Dataset: MIMIC physiological time-series dataset (~25,000 records, six vital signs) with simulated sensor/network anomalies
Used Methods: Deep Autoencoder (AE), Artificial Neural Network (ANN)
XAI: KernelSHAP
Core Methodology: Implements a decentralized two-layer MIoT monitoring framework where edge-based Autoencoders detect anomalies and KernelSHAP explanations are combined with ANN classification at the Local Processing Unit (LPU).
Major Findings: Successfully distinguishes clinical emergencies from technical anomalies while reducing communication overhead and backend latency through edge-based detection.
Critical Limitations: KernelSHAP may become computationally expensive in high-dimensional multimodal healthcare environments, and the Autoencoder may suffer from long-term physiological data drift.
Future Directions: Develop scalable XAI approaches, feature-grouping strategies, self-supervised learning, and continual adaptation mechanisms for dynamic IoMT environments.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it demonstrates how explainable AI and lightweight edge intelligence can reduce false alarms by differentiating cyber-induced anomalies from genuine patient health events in resource-constrained healthcare systems.

Dataset: Not applicable to a single empirical dataset; synthesizes Healthcare-IoT (HC-IoT) literature published between 2015 and 2023.
Used Methods: Systematic Literature Review, Comparative Taxonomy Analysis, Threat Modeling, Structural Vulnerability Analysis
XAI: No explicit XAI implementation; emphasizes the need for transparent logging, auditability, and explainable security mechanisms in healthcare systems.
Core Methodology: Develops a holistic multi-tier security mapping framework that examines vulnerabilities across data acquisition, processing, storage, transmission, and client access layers within Healthcare-IoT ecosystems.
Major Findings: Identifies that wearable biosensors and resource-constrained healthcare devices remain highly vulnerable to attacks such as Sybil, Wormhole, routing manipulation, and anonymity hijacking due to insecure communication channels and fragmented security architectures.
Critical Limitations: Does not provide experimental validation, performance benchmarking, or real-world IDS evaluation metrics. The review is limited to literature published up to 2023 and does not address emerging AI-driven cyberattacks.
Future Directions: Develop lightweight cryptographic mechanisms for constrained healthcare devices, cross-layer security frameworks, adaptive edge-based defenses, and intelligent IDS capable of mitigating evolving multi-vector attacks.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it systematically identifies the architectural attack surfaces, communication-layer vulnerabilities, and threat vectors that future AI-powered IDS solutions must monitor, detect, and mitigate within healthcare environments.

Dataset: CICIoMT2024 dataset containing over 8.7 million traffic records collected from 40 heterogeneous IoMT devices (25 real devices using WiFi/Bluetooth and 15 simulated MQTT devices).
Used Methods: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Deep Learning (DL), Dense Neural Networks
XAI: No XAI technique incorporated; focuses on predictive performance and multi-class attack classification rather than interpretability.
Core Methodology: Proposes the L2D2 architecture consisting of two stacked LSTM layers followed by two dense fully connected layers to capture complex temporal network behaviors and classify benign and malicious IoMT traffic across multiple attack categories.
Major Findings: Achieves approximately 98% multi-class classification accuracy across 19 attack classes and demonstrates the effectiveness of sequential deep learning models for detecting complex attacks including DDoS, DoS, Reconnaissance, MQTT anomalies, and Spoofing in heterogeneous IoMT environments.
Critical Limitations: The recurrent architecture may introduce significant computational overhead and memory requirements for deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. The framework does not investigate feature reduction, model compression, explainability, or cryptographic security integration.
Future Directions: Future work includes integrating advanced feature selection techniques such as Mutual Information and Grey Wolf Optimization, developing online drift-aware learning mechanisms, and adapting the framework for real-time edge deployment.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it provides one of the earliest deep-learning benchmarks on the CICIoMT2024 dataset and demonstrates that LSTM-based architectures can accurately perform fine-grained multi-class attack detection across WiFi, Bluetooth, and MQTT healthcare networks rather than simple binary intrusion classification.

Dataset: Standardization dataset containing 125,973 network traffic records with 41 security and performance-related features.
Used Methods: Fuzzy Delphi Method (FDM), Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM), Borda Voting, VIKOR Ranking, BayesNet, Support Vector Machine (SVM)
XAI: Provides structural transparency through expert-driven MCDM evaluation and consensus-based auditing of classifier selection criteria rather than traditional post-hoc XAI techniques.
Core Methodology: Develops a three-stage standardization framework that uses the Fuzzy Delphi Method to establish expert consensus on IDS evaluation criteria, constructs a decision matrix to assess machine learning models, and applies MCDM with Borda voting and VIKOR ranking to identify the most suitable IDS classifier.
Major Findings: Seventeen of twenty evaluation criteria achieved expert consensus, CPU execution time was identified as the most critical deployment factor, and BayesNet was ranked as the most balanced classifier while SVM received the lowest overall ranking for Federated Learning environments.
Critical Limitations: The framework relies on static evaluation criteria and historical datasets, limiting adaptability to emerging threats and zero-day attacks. The computational complexity of fuzzy consensus processes may also hinder rapid decision updates in real-time deployments.
Future Directions: Future work should focus on adaptive weighting mechanisms, dynamic evaluation frameworks, automated criterion adjustment for evolving threats, and benchmarking advanced deep learning and ensemble IDS models for decentralized healthcare networks.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it provides a formal and standardized framework for IDS model selection, balancing detection performance with resource constraints such as CPU overhead, which is essential for deploying effective intrusion detection systems in Federated Learning and resource-constrained IoMT environments.

Dataset: WUSTL-EHMS-2020 healthcare monitoring dataset containing over 16,000 records integrating biometric measurements and network-flow traffic with Man-In-The-Middle (MITM) spoofing and false data injection attacks.
Used Methods: Random Forest (RF), Decision Tree (DT), Support Vector Classifier (SVC), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Soft Voting Ensemble, ARGUS Network Analysis Framework
XAI: SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) providing both global and local feature attribution to explain intrusion detection decisions and identify the relative contribution of network and biometric features.
Core Methodology: Develops a dual-stage cyber-biomedical intrusion detection pipeline where ARGUS extracts network-flow features and patient biometric data, followed by a soft-voting ensemble combining RF, DT, SVC, and XGBoost classifiers. SHAP is subsequently applied to explain model predictions and validate decision-making processes.
Major Findings: The soft-voting ensemble achieved accuracy and F1-scores exceeding 99.80%, outperforming previous standalone models while demonstrating that combining biometric and network-flow features improves healthcare intrusion detection. SHAP analysis revealed that network-flow metrics dominate general attack detection whereas physiological measurements contribute significantly to spoofing attack identification.
Critical Limitations: Continuous SHAP computation may introduce latency in real-time deployment scenarios, limiting rapid threat response. The evaluation primarily focuses on MITM and false data injection attacks without extensive validation against advanced persistent threats (APTs) or complex multi-vector attacks.
Future Directions: Future research should investigate lightweight explainability techniques, accelerated SHAP approximations, real-time deployment optimization, integration with automated firewall response mechanisms, and validation against broader healthcare cyberattack scenarios.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it demonstrates that fusing biomedical and network traffic features significantly enhances intrusion detection performance while maintaining transparency through SHAP-based explanations, providing a practical framework for trustworthy and clinically deployable IoMT security systems.

Dataset: ECU-IoHT benchmark dataset containing healthcare IoT network traffic generated from realistic medical device environments and common cyberattack scenarios.
Used Methods: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), Deep Neural Networks (DNN), Natural Language Processing (NLP), Deep Learning (DL)
XAI: No explicit SHAP, LIME, or post-hoc XAI method; interpretability is partially achieved through BERT self-attention mechanisms that capture contextual relationships within network traffic sequences.
Core Methodology: Develops a hybrid NLP-DL intrusion detection framework that treats network packets and protocol payloads as textual sequences. A pre-trained BERT model extracts contextual embeddings from network traffic, which are then processed by deep neural classifiers for multi-class intrusion detection.
Major Findings: Achieved 99.11% detection accuracy across five major healthcare cyberattacks and outperformed conventional deep learning models by approximately 2.9%. Demonstrated that transformer-based contextual representations can effectively identify ARP spoofing, DoS, Nmap scanning, and Smurf attacks within healthcare IoT environments.
Critical Limitations: The BERT-based architecture introduces significant computational and memory overhead, making deployment challenging on resource-constrained IoMT devices. Static tokenization and transformer inference may also increase latency under high-volume traffic conditions.
Future Directions: Future research should focus on lightweight transformer architectures such as DistilBERT and MobileBERT, model compression techniques, edge deployment optimization, and Federated Learning integration for privacy-preserving collaborative intrusion detection across healthcare institutions.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it introduces transformer-based language modeling into healthcare intrusion detection, demonstrating that network traffic can be interpreted as contextual language sequences and establishing a new paradigm for advanced multi-class IoMT attack detection using attention-based deep learning architectures.

Dataset: Not applicable to a specific experimental dataset; synthesizes findings from multiple IoMT security studies, healthcare architectures, privacy frameworks, and medical device security publications.
Used Methods: Systematic Literature Review, Qualitative Comparative Analysis, Security Framework Auditing, Taxonomy Construction
XAI: Does not implement a formal XAI technique; promotes transparency through governance, auditable security policies, accountability mechanisms, and explainable decision pathways within healthcare cybersecurity frameworks.
Core Methodology: Proposes a unified IoMT cybersecurity taxonomy organized into three strategic pillars: Govern (risk management, policies, compliance), Protect (access control, cryptography, physical security), and Detect (intrusion detection, anomaly monitoring, threat intelligence), providing an integrated framework for securing medical IoT ecosystems.
Major Findings: Highlights that healthcare organizations frequently prioritize usability over security, identifies fragmented security deployments across multi-vendor IoMT environments, and demonstrates the necessity of unified cross-layer protection strategies to safeguard highly sensitive clinical data.
Critical Limitations: As a survey paper, it lacks experimental validation, benchmark comparisons, and quantitative performance evaluation of specific IDS techniques. It also provides limited consideration of computational constraints associated with deploying security mechanisms on resource-constrained medical devices.
Future Directions: Future research should focus on universal IoMT security standards, automated compliance verification systems, lightweight policy-driven security mechanisms, and integrated governance frameworks capable of supporting diverse healthcare device ecosystems.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it establishes a comprehensive cybersecurity taxonomy that clearly positions intrusion detection within the broader healthcare security lifecycle, providing foundational guidance for designing IDS solutions that align with governance, protection, and regulatory requirements in medical environments.

Dataset: Prominent IoT/IoMT benchmark datasets containing heterogeneous network traffic, Non-IID data distributions, and diverse cyberattack scenarios representative of real-world healthcare environments.
Used Methods: Federated Learning (FL), Deep Learning (DL), Transfer Learning (TL), Federated Averaging (FedAvg), Personalized Model Fine-Tuning
XAI: No explicit SHAP, LIME, or post-hoc explainability method; transparency is partially achieved through Transfer Learning adaptation, allowing analysis of differences between global and local model behaviors across distributed healthcare nodes.
Core Methodology: Proposes a Federated Transfer Learning (FTL) intrusion detection framework where decentralized IoMT gateways collaboratively train a global IDS model through Federated Learning while preserving data privacy. Transfer Learning is subsequently applied to personalize the global model for local healthcare environments and mitigate Non-IID data challenges.
Major Findings: The FTL framework achieved intrusion detection accuracies ranging from 95% to 99%, effectively addressed Non-IID data distribution issues, maintained privacy by avoiding centralized data collection, and demonstrated strong capability in detecting previously unseen zero-day attacks across heterogeneous healthcare networks.
Critical Limitations: Federated training introduces significant communication overhead due to repeated model synchronization rounds, while personalized local fine-tuning increases computational requirements on resource-constrained edge gateways. The framework also remains vulnerable to model-poisoning and adversarial manipulation attacks targeting shared model parameters.
Future Directions: Future work should focus on communication-efficient aggregation methods, lightweight federated optimization, differential privacy integration, homomorphic encryption, secure aggregation protocols, and defenses against model-poisoning attacks in healthcare Federated Learning environments.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it demonstrates how Federated Learning and Transfer Learning can be combined to build privacy-preserving intrusion detection systems capable of handling heterogeneous Non-IID healthcare data while maintaining high detection performance and improving resilience against zero-day attacks without exposing sensitive patient information.

Dataset: WUSTL-EHMS-2020 dataset containing healthcare biometric measurements and network-flow traffic records with Man-In-The-Middle (MITM) and false data injection attack scenarios.
Used Methods: Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), Ensemble Learning, Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) Edge Architecture
XAI: SHAP (SHapley Additive Explanations) used to provide post-hoc feature attribution and explain the influence of network-flow and physiological features on intrusion detection decisions.
Core Methodology: Develops a three-tier cloud-to-edge intrusion detection framework that processes multimodal IoMT data, applies Particle Swarm Optimization for feature selection and dimensionality reduction, deploys ensemble classifiers on edge nodes through a SaaS architecture, and utilizes SHAP to ensure transparent and interpretable decision-making.
Major Findings: PSO-based feature optimization significantly reduces computational overhead while maintaining high detection performance, outperforming conventional standalone machine learning models on the WUSTL-EHMS-2020 dataset. The framework also improves analyst trust by providing actionable explanations through SHAP-based feature attribution.
Critical Limitations: Particle Swarm Optimization may become trapped in local optima when processing highly complex and high-dimensional healthcare traffic. Dependence on SaaS infrastructure also introduces reliance on stable cloud-edge connectivity and may create operational vulnerabilities during service disruptions.
Future Directions: Future work should explore hybrid optimization approaches combining PSO with Genetic Algorithms or Grey Wolf Optimization, adaptive online feature selection, continuous learning mechanisms, and autonomous edge-level optimization without requiring centralized recalibration.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it demonstrates how metaheuristic feature optimization can reduce resource consumption while maintaining high intrusion detection accuracy and explainability, providing a scalable framework for deploying transparent AI-driven IDS solutions on resource-constrained healthcare edge devices.

Dataset: IoTID20 and Edge-IIoTset datasets containing diverse IoT traffic and contemporary cyberattacks including DDoS, DoS, scanning, and botnet activities.
Used Methods: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Deep Learning (DL), Fog Computing, Edge Deployment
XAI: No explicit SHAP, LIME, or post-hoc explainability mechanism; model transparency is limited to performance monitoring and fog-layer operational telemetry.
Core Methodology: Develops the HIDS-IoMT framework, a fog-based intrusion detection architecture that processes network traffic locally, extracts spatial features using CNN layers, models temporal attack behavior through LSTM layers, and deploys the complete IDS pipeline on a Raspberry Pi fog gateway for real-time healthcare security monitoring.
Major Findings: Achieved 99.92% accuracy, 99.91% precision, 99.99% recall, and 99.95% F1-score while successfully detecting DDoS, DoS, SQL injection, vulnerability scanning, port scanning, and Mirai botnet attacks. Demonstrated that hybrid CNN-LSTM models can be deployed effectively on low-cost edge hardware with reduced latency and cloud dependency.
Critical Limitations: The framework was evaluated using generic IoT traffic datasets rather than real medical sensor protocols such as DICOM or HL7. LSTM components may also experience scalability and memory limitations when deployed in large-scale hospital environments with high traffic volumes.
Future Directions: Future work should investigate lightweight architectures such as GRU and attention-based models, model compression techniques, adaptive online learning, zero-day attack detection, and integration with real-world healthcare communication protocols.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it provides a practical fog-computing deployment blueprint showing that high-performance deep learning IDS models can operate on resource-constrained edge hardware while maintaining near state-of-the-art detection accuracy for healthcare-oriented cyberattacks.

Dataset: CIC-DDoS2019 dataset containing large-scale multi-protocol DDoS traffic including DNS, UDP, UDP-Lag, NTP, and SYN flooding attacks.
Used Methods: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Deep Learning (DL), Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL) Security
XAI: No explicit SHAP, LIME, or post-hoc explainability technique; transparency is limited to protocol monitoring logs, classification outputs, and performance evaluation metrics.
Core Methodology: Develops the HIDS-RPL framework for protecting RPL-based IoMT environments by capturing routing traffic logs, extracting spatial traffic characteristics using CNN layers, and modeling temporal attack behaviors using LSTM networks to detect routing and flooding attacks in low-power healthcare networks.
Major Findings: Achieved 99.87% accuracy, 98.50% precision, 98.64% recall, and 98.54% F1-score while demonstrating strong detection capability against DNS, UDP, UDP-Lag, NTP, and SYN flooding attacks. The framework shows that hybrid CNN-LSTM models can effectively secure low-power medical communication environments against large-scale DDoS threats.
Critical Limitations: The framework was evaluated primarily on CIC-DDoS2019 traffic and lacks validation against specialized RPL routing attacks such as Rank attacks, Version Number attacks, and DIS flooding attacks. Continuous CNN-LSTM processing may also create computational overhead for highly constrained medical sensor devices.
Future Directions: Future work should investigate lightweight architectures such as 1D-CNNs and GRUs, optimize energy-efficient edge deployment, and expand evaluation to include protocol-specific routing attacks targeting dynamic IoMT network topologies.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it focuses on securing RPL-based low-power medical communication networks and demonstrates that hybrid CNN-LSTM architectures can provide highly accurate protection against DDoS attacks that threaten the availability and reliability of healthcare IoT infrastructures.

Dataset: Not applicable to a single experimental dataset; synthesizes findings from multiple IoT, healthcare, enterprise security, and Federated Learning IDS studies across diverse benchmark environments.
Used Methods: Systematic Literature Review, Federated Learning (FL), Architectural Taxonomy Mapping, Threat Modeling, Comparative Analysis, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Hybrid Deep Learning
XAI: Discusses Explainable AI as a critical trust-building component in Federated IDS ecosystems, emphasizing transparent model updates, interpretable decision-making, and auditable aggregation processes rather than implementing a specific XAI technique.
Core Methodology: Develops a comprehensive taxonomy of Federated Learning-based Intrusion Detection Systems by analyzing decentralized training architectures, aggregation mechanisms, hybrid deep learning models, GAN-enhanced frameworks, and privacy-preserving collaborative security strategies across distributed environments.
Major Findings: Demonstrates that Federated Learning enables effective intrusion detection while preserving privacy by avoiding centralized data collection. Highlights the effectiveness of hybrid deep learning, GAN-enhanced IDS architectures, and decentralized learning strategies for protecting sensitive healthcare information. Also identifies Non-IID data heterogeneity as a major challenge affecting global model performance and convergence.
Critical Limitations: Does not provide experimental validation, hardware benchmarking, or deployment-level performance measurements. Existing Federated Learning approaches such as FedAvg remain vulnerable to communication inefficiencies, slow convergence, and reduced performance under highly heterogeneous client data distributions.
Future Directions: Future research should focus on communication-efficient aggregation methods, robust Non-IID learning strategies, scalable privacy-preserving architectures, secure federated optimization, adversarial resilience, and explainable federated IDS frameworks for healthcare environments.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it provides a comprehensive roadmap for privacy-preserving Federated IDS design, highlighting how decentralized collaborative learning, GAN-enhanced architectures, and advanced aggregation mechanisms can protect sensitive medical data while maintaining effective intrusion detection across distributed healthcare networks.

Dataset: CIC-IDS2017, CSE-CIC-IDS2018, LycoS-IDS2017, and LycoS-Unicas-IDS2018 datasets containing diverse network intrusion traffic and cross-environment attack scenarios.
Used Methods: Random Forest (RF), Decision Tree (DT), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), t-SNE Visualization, Cross-Dataset Evaluation
XAI: No explicit SHAP, LIME, or post-hoc explainability framework; transparency is achieved through feature-space visualization, statistical analysis, and t-SNE-based examination of dataset distributions and model behavior across domains.
Core Methodology: Develops a cross-dataset generalization evaluation framework that compares within-dataset and cross-dataset performance by training machine learning models on one dataset and testing them on entirely different datasets while analyzing feature distribution shifts and dataset-specific artifacts.
Major Findings: Demonstrates that machine learning models achieve near-perfect performance under traditional within-dataset evaluation but suffer severe performance degradation during cross-dataset testing, revealing substantial generalization failures caused by dataset bias, feature drift, and network-specific artifacts.
Critical Limitations: The study highlights that conventional benchmark evaluations can create misleading perceptions of IDS effectiveness due to overfitting to dataset-specific characteristics. The evaluation is limited to classical machine learning models and does not investigate modern deep learning, transformer-based, or foundation-model architectures.
Future Directions: Future work should focus on invariant feature learning, domain adaptation, transfer learning, cross-domain representation learning, decentralized collaborative learning, and robust evaluation methodologies capable of improving generalization across heterogeneous network environments.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it directly exposes the generalization problem that threatens real-world deployment of intrusion detection systems. The findings demonstrate that high benchmark accuracy does not guarantee operational effectiveness across different healthcare environments, highlighting the need for domain adaptation and cross-dataset validation in future IoMT IDS research.

Dataset: CICIoT2023 and CICIoMT2024 datasets containing general IoT and specialized Medical IoT network traffic with multiple attack categories and communication protocols.
Used Methods: Machine Learning (ML), Feature Engineering, Cross-Dataset Validation, Temporal Windowing, Data Rebalancing, Performance Auditing
XAI: No explicit SHAP, LIME, or post-hoc explainability framework; transparency is achieved through systematic analysis of dataset biases, train-test leakage, temporal dependencies, and data quality issues affecting IDS evaluation.
Core Methodology: Develops a rigorous dataset evaluation and reconstruction framework that performs reciprocal cross-dataset validation between CICIoT2023 and CICIoMT2024, identifies hidden benchmark flaws, corrects temporal and sampling inconsistencies, and proposes standardized preprocessing and balancing procedures for reliable IDS development.
Major Findings: Demonstrates a severe cross-domain performance degradation of up to 66.87% in F1-score when models trained on general IoT traffic are evaluated on specialized IoMT environments. Reveals critical flaws within CICIoMT2024, including temporal dependency violations and sampling leakage, and shows that correcting these issues enables classification performance reaching 99.85% accuracy.
Critical Limitations: The proposed improvements were evaluated only under offline experimental settings and were not validated on real-time edge deployments. The study also does not assess the computational overhead of the preprocessing pipeline on resource-constrained medical devices or embedded healthcare gateways.
Future Directions: Future work should focus on adaptive real-time preprocessing, online temporal windowing strategies, validation on edge-computing platforms, federated learning integration, and evaluation using advanced deep learning and transformer-based IDS architectures.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it proves that general IoT datasets are insufficient proxies for healthcare security environments, exposes critical weaknesses within CICIoMT2024 benchmarking practices, and provides essential guidelines for building trustworthy, unbiased, and generalizable intrusion detection systems specifically tailored to Medical IoT ecosystems.

Dataset: Four benchmark IoMT and healthcare intrusion detection datasets including WUSTL-EHMS-2020 and related medical network traffic environments evaluated under IID data distributions.
Used Methods: Federated Learning (FL), Meta-Learning, Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks (KAN), KANConvNet, Clustering-Based Aggregation, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)
XAI: Provides inherent interpretability through Kolmogorov–Arnold Network (KAN) architecture, where learnable B-spline activation functions enable transparent modeling of feature interactions without requiring post-hoc explainability methods such as SHAP or LIME.
Core Methodology: Develops the FedIoMT framework, which combines secure federated learning, KANConvNet local classifiers, meta-learning strategies, and clustering-based aggregation to improve intrusion detection performance while defending against model-poisoning attacks in distributed healthcare environments.
Major Findings: Achieved classification accuracies of 99.38%, 99.23%, 99.26%, and 99.20% across four benchmark datasets. Demonstrated improved parameter efficiency and scalability through KANConvNet while successfully detecting and mitigating poisoned model updates through clustering-based aggregation mechanisms.
Critical Limitations: The framework was primarily evaluated under IID data distributions and lacks extensive validation on realistic Non-IID healthcare environments. Meta-learning and repeated local training rounds may also increase computational requirements for resource-constrained wearable and edge healthcare devices.
Future Directions: Future research should investigate Non-IID federated learning scenarios, lightweight KAN optimization techniques, model quantization, pruning strategies, communication-efficient aggregation methods, and deployment on ultra-low-power healthcare devices.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it introduces Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks into federated intrusion detection, demonstrating that inherently interpretable, parameter-efficient, and privacy-preserving architectures can achieve high detection performance while improving resilience against model-poisoning attacks in distributed healthcare ecosystems.

Dataset: CICIDS2017, ToN_IoT, and a Windows malware dataset covering network intrusion traffic, IoT/IoMT telemetry, and endpoint malware scenarios.
Used Methods: Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), Transformer, Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), Ensemble Tree Boosting
XAI: No explicit SHAP, LIME, or post-hoc explainability framework; transparency is achieved through architectural separation between network intrusion detection and endpoint malware detection components as well as the interpretable structure of tree-based models.
Core Methodology: Develops a dual-engine healthcare security architecture consisting of a LightGBM-based Intrusion Detection System (IDS) for analyzing IoMT and network traffic and a Transformer-based Malware Detection System (MDS) for detecting malicious activities on healthcare endpoints, servers, and clinical workstations.
Major Findings: The LightGBM-based IDS achieved approximately 99% accuracy and F1-score across network intrusion datasets, while the Transformer-based malware detection engine achieved approximately 99% accuracy in identifying modern Windows malware. The framework demonstrates that combining specialized models for different security layers improves overall healthcare infrastructure protection.
Critical Limitations: The Transformer component introduces significant computational and memory overhead, limiting deployment on resource-constrained devices. The framework was not evaluated on specialized healthcare communication protocols such as HL7 or DICOM and lacks validation using direct medical device traffic streams.
Future Directions: Future work should focus on lightweight Transformer architectures, model compression and distillation techniques, optimized healthcare protocol support, streaming medical sensor integration, and resource-efficient deployment strategies for healthcare environments.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it demonstrates that effective healthcare cybersecurity requires separate but coordinated protection mechanisms for network-layer intrusion detection and endpoint malware defense, providing a practical blueprint for multi-layer AI-driven healthcare security architectures.

Dataset: UNSW-NB15 dataset and a newly developed healthcare-specific anomaly detection dataset containing IoT attack traffic, healthcare telemetry, biometric data manipulation scenarios, and healthcare-oriented cyberattacks.
Used Methods: Random Forest (RF), Artificial Neural Network (ANN), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Stacking Ensemble Learning, Machine Learning (ML)
XAI: No explicit SHAP, LIME, or post-hoc explainability framework; transparency is achieved through the documented stacking architecture where RF and ANN predictions are combined and interpreted by an XGBoost meta-learner.
Core Methodology: Develops a real-time anomaly detection framework that pre-trains Random Forest and ANN base models, combines their outputs through an XGBoost stacking meta-learner, and deploys the architecture within a simulated edge computing environment for continuous healthcare traffic monitoring and anomaly detection.
Major Findings: The stacking ensemble significantly outperformed standalone classifiers across accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score metrics while successfully detecting healthcare-specific threats such as biometric data falsification and denial-of-service attacks. The framework also demonstrated the ability to process real-time streaming data without introducing significant queue delays.
Critical Limitations: The edge deployment was validated only through simulation rather than on physical embedded hardware, leaving memory, power consumption, and latency constraints unverified. The supervised learning architecture may also struggle to detect previously unseen zero-day attacks without retraining.
Future Directions: Future research should focus on deployment on real edge devices, self-supervised and unsupervised anomaly detection mechanisms, lightweight model optimization, adaptive online learning, and improved zero-day attack detection capabilities for healthcare environments.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it introduces a healthcare-specific anomaly detection dataset and demonstrates that stacking ensemble architectures combining RF, ANN, and XGBoost can provide accurate, low-latency detection of healthcare-focused attacks in real-time streaming environments while supporting edge-oriented deployment strategies.

Dataset: Meta-analysis of 15 benchmark datasets including CICIDS2017, UNSW-NB15, NSL-KDD, ToN-IoT, BoT-IoT, Edge-IIoT, WUSTL-EHMS, Ecu-IoHT, ICE, and BlueTack.
Used Methods: Systematic Literature Review, Taxonomy Construction, Threat Modeling, Cloud-Fog-Edge Mapping, Random Forest (RF), Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Deep Neural Networks (DNN), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), Genetic Algorithms (GA)
XAI: Identifies Explainable AI (XAI) as an emerging requirement for trustworthy healthcare intrusion detection and discusses the integration of explainable mechanisms with deep learning architectures such as bidirectional Simple Recurrent Units (bid-SRU) to improve stakeholder confidence and decision transparency.
Core Methodology: Develops a comprehensive IoMT security taxonomy spanning perception, network, transport, and application layers while mapping machine learning tasks including preprocessing, feature selection, classification, and anomaly detection across Cloud, Fog, and Edge computing environments.
Major Findings: Demonstrates that Random Forest remains one of the most widely adopted and effective machine learning approaches for IoMT intrusion detection, particularly when combined with optimization techniques such as PSO and GA. Also highlights that hybrid deep learning architectures combining CNN and LSTM models consistently achieve superior detection performance across healthcare environments.
Critical Limitations: As a survey study, it does not provide original experimental validation or novel model development. The review also identifies a major limitation in existing research where many intrusion detection models are evaluated using generic network datasets that do not accurately represent healthcare communication protocols such as MQTT, CoAP, HL7, and DICOM.
Future Directions: Future research should focus on lightweight AI models for embedded medical devices, continuous online learning systems, adaptive zero-day attack detection, protocol-aware intrusion detection, explainable AI integration, and resource-efficient healthcare security architectures suitable for Cloud-Fog-Edge environments.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it provides a comprehensive map of the IoMT intrusion detection landscape, identifies major dataset and protocol gaps, summarizes effective machine learning and deep learning approaches, and establishes a structured roadmap for developing scalable, explainable, and clinically compliant intrusion detection systems across healthcare infrastructures.

Dataset: WUSTL-EHMS-2020 dataset containing 35 network-flow features and 8 biometric features across 16,318 healthcare monitoring instances, including both normal and attack traffic.
Used Methods: Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE), Random Forest (RF), Hybrid Random Sampling, Machine Learning (ML), Grid Search Optimization
XAI: SHAP and LIME used for both global and local explainability. SHAP identifies globally important features while LIME provides instance-level explanations for individual intrusion detection decisions.
Core Methodology: Develops a five-stage explainable intrusion detection framework involving data preprocessing, hybrid class balancing, feature selection using RFE, hyperparameter optimization of XGBoost, and explainability analysis through SHAP and LIME to create a transparent healthcare intrusion detection system.
Major Findings: Achieved 99.22% accuracy, 98.35% precision, 99.91% recall, 99.12% F1-score, and 100% ROC-AUC. Demonstrated that combining biometric and network features improves intrusion detection performance and reduces false alarms, while SHAP and LIME provide detailed explanations of model behavior.
Critical Limitations: The framework was evaluated only in an offline environment and lacks validation on resource-constrained medical devices. The use of SHAP and LIME may introduce computational overhead and latency when deployed in real-time healthcare monitoring systems.
Future Directions: Future research should investigate model compression, pruning, quantization, healthcare-specific explainability methods, counterfactual reasoning, causal AI, adversarial robustness, and deployment on low-power healthcare devices.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it provides a high-performance explainable intrusion detection framework that combines network traffic analysis with patient biometric information while delivering transparent decision-making through SHAP and LIME, supporting trustworthy and clinically acceptable healthcare cybersecurity systems.

Dataset: CICDDoS2019 dataset containing large-scale multi-class DDoS traffic, reflection attacks, and exploitation-based flooding attacks across multiple network protocols.
Used Methods: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Deep Neural Network (DNN), cuLSTM-DNN, cuGRU-DNN, cuCNN-GRU, Deep Learning (DL), Software-Defined Networking (SDN), CUDA GPU Acceleration
XAI: No explicit SHAP, LIME, or post-hoc explainability mechanism; transparency is provided through SDN control-plane visibility and structured network orchestration rather than model-level interpretability.
Core Methodology: Develops a softwarized healthcare security framework that integrates Software-Defined Networking with a CUDA-accelerated cuLSTM-DNN intrusion detection engine. Network traffic is managed through an SDN controller and analyzed using GPU-accelerated deep learning models to achieve high-speed multi-class attack detection within IoT-enabled smart healthcare environments.
Major Findings: Achieved 99.62% average detection accuracy, 99.13% recall, 99.47% F1-score, and 99.24% precision on CICDDoS2019. The framework reached a peak accuracy of 99.92% and achieved ultra-low inference latency of approximately 13.7 milliseconds, demonstrating the effectiveness of GPU-accelerated deep learning for real-time healthcare intrusion detection.
Critical Limitations: The architecture depends heavily on GPU acceleration and CUDA-enabled hardware, limiting deployment on low-cost and resource-constrained healthcare edge devices. The evaluation also focuses primarily on network-layer attacks and does not incorporate biometric data, healthcare-specific protocols, or physiological monitoring streams.
Future Directions: Future research should investigate lightweight and distilled deep learning architectures, edge-friendly acceleration techniques, protocol-aware healthcare intrusion detection, integration of medical communication standards such as HL7 and DICOM, and deployment on resource-constrained healthcare gateways.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it demonstrates how Software-Defined Networking and GPU-accelerated deep learning can dramatically reduce intrusion detection latency while maintaining near state-of-the-art accuracy, providing a practical framework for real-time security monitoring in smart healthcare infrastructures.

Dataset: Synthetic Gaussian dataset containing 15,000 instances and a real-world VitalCore healthcare dataset monitoring connection status data from more than 3,000 medical devices using six-dimensional telemetry features.
Used Methods: One-Class Support Vector Machine (OC-SVM), Autoencoder, Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) Learning, Statistical Learning Theory, Semi-Supervised Anomaly Detection
XAI: Provides interpretability through mathematically provable performance guarantees rather than post-hoc explanations. The framework explicitly controls False Alarm Rate (FAR) and Miss Alarm Rate (MAR) using user-defined confidence and error bounds, making model behavior transparent and auditable.
Core Methodology: Develops a human-in-the-loop anomaly detection framework that uses PAC-learning theory to establish bounded uncertainty regions through separate calibration sets for normal behavior, expected anomalies, and unexpected anomalies. Detection thresholds are continuously refined using low-frequency expert feedback while maintaining formal performance guarantees.
Major Findings: Demonstrates that PAC-based calibration can maintain a strict error guarantee of ε = 0.02 while reducing uncertainty to below 2%. The framework substantially reduces false alarm rates compared with traditional approaches and shows that approximately one expert feedback event per week is sufficient to achieve near-optimal performance and continuous adaptation.
Critical Limitations: The framework assumes relatively stable baseline data distributions and depends on a clean initial training dataset. Significant long-term behavioral drift may require retraining and recalibration, while the semi-supervised design remains dependent on initial baseline quality.
Future Directions: Future research should focus on continuous adaptation mechanisms, online learning strategies, long-term drift management, enhanced human-feedback integration, user-centered explainability tools, and deployment in dynamic healthcare environments with evolving attack patterns.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it introduces mathematically guaranteed anomaly detection through PAC-learning theory, offering a rigorous framework for controlling false alarms and missed detections in safety-critical healthcare systems where reliability, trust, and regulatory compliance are as important as detection accuracy.

Dataset: Meta-analysis of multiple healthcare and IoT security benchmarks including WUSTL-EHMS, ToN-IoT, CICIDS, and simulated healthcare routing attack environments developed using the Contiki-OS COOJA simulator.
Used Methods: Systematic Literature Review, Threat Taxonomy Development, Qualitative Risk Assessment, COOJA Simulation Modeling, Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL)
XAI: Identifies Explainable AI as a critical requirement for trustworthy healthcare intrusion detection and emphasizes transparent logging, auditable verification, and interpretable AI systems to support clinical decision-making and automated threat mitigation.

The framework categorizes 26 distinct attack types and evaluates mitigation strategies while leveraging COOJA simulation to model routing attacks and wireless communication vulnerabilities in healthcare environments.
Major Findings: Demonstrates that machine learning and deep learning techniques can effectively automate threat detection, authentication, and vulnerability assessment across Healthcare-IoT infrastructures. Highlights the value of simulation environments such as COOJA for evaluating routing attacks and communication-layer vulnerabilities without requiring costly physical deployments.
Critical Limitations: As a survey and taxonomy study, it does not provide new experimental validation or introduce a novel IDS model. The study also identifies persistent challenges related to interoperability, real-time detection performance, and protection of heterogeneous multi-vendor healthcare ecosystems.
Future Directions: Future research should focus on lightweight edge-based IDS architectures, adaptive cross-layer defense mechanisms, explainable AI integration, protection against AI-driven cyberattacks, secure 5G-enabled healthcare infrastructures, and scalable intrusion detection for heterogeneous healthcare environments.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it provides one of the most comprehensive Healthcare-IoT threat taxonomies available, mapping 26 attack categories across multiple architectural layers and offering a structured blueprint for designing resilient, explainable, and multi-layer intrusion detection systems for healthcare networks.

Dataset: CIC-IDS2017 dataset containing benign traffic and multiple contemporary cyberattack categories including Botnet, Brute Force, DoS/DDoS, and Web Attacks.
Used Methods: Deep Belief Network (DBN), Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM), Deep Learning (DL), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), Spiking Neural Network (SNN)
XAI: No explicit SHAP, LIME, or post-hoc explainability framework; transparency is derived from the hierarchical feature-learning process of stacked Restricted Boltzmann Machines and the structured architecture of the Deep Belief Network.
Core Methodology: Develops a multi-class intrusion detection framework based on Deep Belief Networks, where multiple Restricted Boltzmann Machine layers perform unsupervised feature extraction and hierarchical representation learning before supervised fine-tuning through backpropagation for attack classification.
Major Findings: Achieved high multi-class detection performance with 99.37% accuracy for Botnet attacks, 97.71% for Brute Force attacks, 96.67% for DoS/DDoS attacks, and 98.37% for Web Attacks. The DBN consistently outperformed traditional machine learning models and alternative neural architectures while maintaining stable performance above 95% across all evaluated attack categories.
Critical Limitations: The framework was evaluated using offline datasets and does not address deployment constraints such as energy consumption, memory requirements, or computational limitations of healthcare edge devices. It also lacks evaluation against zero-day attacks, adversarial manipulation, and healthcare-specific threat scenarios.
Future Directions: Future work should focus on model compression, quantization, edge deployment optimization, adversarial robustness, zero-day attack detection, and adaptation of Deep Belief Networks to healthcare-specific intrusion detection scenarios involving medical devices and physiological data streams.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it represents an important milestone in the evolution of deep learning-based intrusion detection, demonstrating the effectiveness of unsupervised hierarchical feature learning through Deep Belief Networks and providing a foundational benchmark that influenced later deep learning architectures used in healthcare cybersecurity systems.

Demonstrated that combining metaheuristic feature optimization with deep auto-encoder architectures improves detection performance while reducing redundancy and overall model complexity.
Critical Limitations: The IGTO optimization process may introduce significant computational overhead and latency during feature selection, limiting applicability in real-time healthcare environments. Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it demonstrates how advanced metaheuristic feature selection combined with deep auto-encoder architectures can improve intrusion detection performance while reducing feature redundancy, offering a promising direction for building efficient AI-driven intrusion detection systems in resource-constrained healthcare environments.

Dataset: CIC IoMT dataset containing multi-protocol WiFi and MQTT healthcare traffic with imbalanced attack distributions and multiple IoMT cyberthreat categories.
Used Methods: UNet++, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Deep Learning (DL), Quantile Transformer, Multi-Class Classification
XAI: Investigates explainability indirectly by comparing the hybrid deep learning framework against interpretable Decision Tree models, highlighting the trade-off between classification performance and transparency in healthcare security applications.
Core Methodology: Develops a hybrid dual-branch intrusion detection architecture where network traffic features are first normalized using a Quantile Transformer, then processed simultaneously through a UNet++ branch for multi-scale spatial feature extraction and an LSTM branch for temporal sequence learning. The outputs are fused and passed to a final classification layer for anomaly and attack identification.
Major Findings: Achieved 99.92% accuracy, 99.997% precision, and 0.9992 ROC-AUC for binary anomaly detection. For complex 19-class attack classification, the model achieved 87.96% accuracy and 86.47% F1-score, substantially outperforming traditional Random Forest and AdaBoost baselines while effectively detecting diverse WiFi and MQTT-based IoMT attacks.
Critical Limitations: The framework exhibits performance degradation when distinguishing between certain low-frequency attack classes such as ARP spoofing and port scanning due to class imbalance and traffic similarity. Additionally, evaluation was conducted offline and does not assess memory usage, latency, or deployment feasibility on resource-constrained healthcare edge devices.
Future Directions: Future research should investigate class-weighting strategies, imbalance-aware learning, model compression, edge deployment optimization, online learning, and lightweight versions of the UNet++-LSTM architecture capable of real-time healthcare intrusion detection.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it demonstrates that computer vision-inspired architectures such as UNet++ can be successfully adapted for healthcare network security, achieving strong performance across 19 attack categories and establishing a promising direction for hybrid spatial-temporal intrusion detection models in multi-protocol IoMT environments.

Dataset: WUSTL-EHMS, IoT-ICU, and ECU-IoHT datasets containing healthcare-oriented network traffic, multi-protocol communications, and diverse cyberattack categories.
Used Methods: Enhanced Multigrained Scanning-Based Deep Stacking Network (MGDSN), Deep Stacking Network (DSN), Ensemble Learning, Deep Learning (DL), Mutual Information Feature Selection

Major Findings: Achieved state-of-the-art performance across WUSTL-EHMS, IoT-ICU, and ECU-IoHT datasets, outperforming alternative deep learning and ensemble approaches including DBN, XSRU, and SAE-XGBoost. Demonstrated near-perfect ROC characteristics and achieved zero classification error on selected attack detection tasks within IoT-ICU and WUSTL-EHMS environments.
Critical Limitations: The framework may introduce computational overhead due to repeated sliding-window feature extraction and multi-layer stacking operations. The supervised feature-selection mechanism also depends on labeled data, potentially limiting effectiveness against previously unseen zero-day attacks and evolving threat patterns.
Future Directions: Future research should focus on lightweight multigrained scanning techniques, edge-oriented optimization, self-supervised learning, unsupervised anomaly detection, domain adaptation, and efficient deployment on resource-constrained healthcare devices.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it demonstrates that deep ensemble architectures combined with multigrained feature extraction can significantly improve healthcare intrusion detection performance, providing an effective framework for detecting diverse IoMT attacks such as ARP spoofing, Smurf flooding, and Nmap scanning while overcoming limitations of conventional deep learning architectures.

Dataset: CIC-DDoS2019, CICIoT2023, and MOCAST2023 datasets representing network flooding attacks, large-scale IoT environments, and 5G core network infrastructures.
Used Methods: Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), ANOVA F-Test Feature Selection, Machine Learning (ML), SHAP, LIME, Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)
XAI: Employs a dual-layer explainability framework combining global and local SHAP explanations with LIME-based local interpretation. Introduces cross-validation between SHAP and LIME explanations to assess explanation consistency and incorporates explanation-generation latency as an evaluation metric.
Core Methodology: Develops a two-stage explainable intrusion detection framework where ANOVA feature selection and global SHAP importance analysis reduce feature dimensionality by approximately 70%, retaining only the most informative features. The reduced feature set is then used to train an optimized XGBoost classifier, while SHAP and LIME are applied to validate and explain model decisions.
Major Findings: Achieved near-perfect classification performance with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-scores ranging from 99.9% to 100% across multiple datasets. Demonstrated that reducing dimensionality by 70% preserved detection performance while significantly improving computational efficiency. Also showed that LIME generated explanations substantially faster than SHAP, making it more suitable for latency-sensitive environments.
Critical Limitations: Explanation consistency issues may arise when SHAP and LIME provide conflicting interpretations for certain features. The framework also relies on supervised learning and may struggle to detect previously unseen zero-day attacks without retraining or adaptation mechanisms.
Future Directions: Future research should evaluate explanation consistency in deep learning and transformer-based architectures, investigate real-time edge deployment, assess explanation overhead in streaming environments, and explore adaptive intrusion detection mechanisms capable of handling emerging attack patterns.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it addresses one of the major barriers to explainable healthcare cybersecurity: computational overhead. The framework demonstrates that aggressive feature reduction combined with validated explainability can deliver highly accurate, efficient, and trustworthy intrusion detection suitable for resource-constrained healthcare and IoMT environments.

Highlights the effectiveness of edge and fog computing combined with deep learning for reducing latency and preserving privacy while maintaining strong intrusion detection performance.

Used Methods: Systematic Literature Review, Federated Learning (FL), Architectural Taxonomy Development, Threat Modeling, Privacy-Preserving Learning, Federated Transfer Learning, Horizontal FL, Vertical FL
XAI: Highlights Explainable AI as a critical requirement for trustworthy Federated Learning-based healthcare intrusion detection systems, emphasizing the need for interpretable local decisions and transparent aggregation mechanisms to support clinician trust and security auditing.

Major Findings: The FCM-SVM framework achieved the highest binary classification performance on UNSW-NB15 with an accuracy of 99.954%, while the SVM-ANN hybrid achieved the best multi-class performance on NSL-KDD with an accuracy of 99.362%. The study demonstrates that combining clustering techniques with machine learning classifiers can significantly improve intrusion detection effectiveness.
Critical Limitations: The proposed models rely on centralized offline training and do not address deployment constraints associated with edge computing environments. Future Directions: Future work should investigate lightweight deep learning architectures, online learning mechanisms, adaptive intrusion detection, edge deployment optimization, healthcare-specific validation, and detection of evolving zero-day attack patterns.

Major Findings: The PSO-Random Forest model achieved the best overall performance with 99.76% accuracy, 99.75% precision, 96.45% recall, and 99.51% MCC. Feature optimization substantially reduced training time, with several models training in less than 0.12 seconds. Traditional machine learning classifiers consistently outperformed the deep RNN model across most evaluation metrics.
Critical Limitations: The framework was validated only on the legacy NSL-KDD dataset, limiting its applicability to modern IoMT environments. It lacks healthcare-specific traffic, medical communication protocols, and mechanisms for detecting zero-day or evolving attacks.
Future Directions: Future work should investigate blockchain-enabled intrusion detection, online adaptive feature selection, edge deployment optimization, healthcare-specific benchmarking, and dynamic intrusion detection capable of handling emerging attack patterns.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it demonstrates the importance of feature optimization for resource-constrained environments. The study shows that metaheuristic feature selection combined with lightweight machine learning models can achieve excellent detection performance with very low computational cost, making it a valuable reference for designing efficient IDS solutions for healthcare and IoMT networks.

Dataset: Simulated healthcare network environments containing custom radio-level communication traffic and physiological ECG telemetry datasets representing realistic patient monitoring scenarios.
Used Methods: Decision Tree (DT), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Naive Bayes Classifier (NBC), k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Random Forest (RF), Polynomial Regression (PR), Mobile Agent Computing, Machine Learning (ML)
XAI: No explicit SHAP, LIME, or post-hoc explainability framework; transparency is achieved through rule-based mobile agent operations, interpretable Decision Tree models, and clearly defined distributed monitoring workflows.
Core Methodology: Develops a distributed mobile-agent intrusion detection framework for healthcare environments. Lightweight Sensor Agents carrying minimal state information are deployed across network nodes to perform decentralized monitoring. Decision Trees are used for network intrusion detection, while Polynomial Regression models profile physiological signals and identify device-level anomalies and potential data manipulation attempts.
Major Findings: Achieved 99.6% network intrusion detection accuracy and 98.2% device-level anomaly detection accuracy. Decision Trees outperformed alternative machine learning models due to low computational complexity, low false-positive rates, and suitability for energy-constrained healthcare environments. The mobile-agent architecture significantly reduced communication and computational overhead.
Critical Limitations: The framework experiences performance degradation against adaptive adversaries that dynamically alter attack behavior. Polynomial Regression also struggles to accurately model highly complex and irregular physiological patterns compared to more advanced sequence-learning techniques.
Future Directions: Future work should focus on real-world deployment on healthcare edge devices, adaptive learning mechanisms, advanced time-series models for physiological monitoring, energy-aware optimization, and integration with modern deep learning architectures for dynamic anomaly detection.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it demonstrates one of the earliest energy-efficient distributed intrusion detection architectures specifically designed for healthcare environments. The study provides a practical blueprint for decentralized monitoring of both network traffic and physiological data while maintaining extremely low resource consumption, which remains a critical requirement for wearable and battery-powered medical devices.

Dataset: NSL-KDD and CICIDS2018 datasets representing both traditional and modern network intrusion environments with diverse attack categories and large-scale traffic profiles.
Used Methods: Decision Tree (DT), k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Artificial Neural Network (ANN), Random Forest (RF), Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), Weighted Ensemble Learning, Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL)
XAI: No explicit SHAP, LIME, or post-hoc explainability framework; transparency is achieved through interpretable tree-based classifiers and documented PSO-derived weighting coefficients used within the ensemble optimization process.
Core Methodology: Develops an adaptive weighted ensemble intrusion detection framework where multiple base classifiers (DT, KNN, ANN, and RF) are independently trained and subsequently combined using Particle Swarm Optimization to identify the optimal classifier weights. The PSO algorithm continuously searches for the best ensemble configuration to maximize overall detection performance.
Major Findings: Achieved 99.83% accuracy and 99.90% F1-score on NSL-KDD, as well as 99.91% accuracy and 99.81% F1-score on CICIDS2018. Ablation studies demonstrated that removing the PSO optimization layer reduced performance by approximately 1.5%, confirming the importance of metaheuristic ensemble optimization for improving classification stability and accuracy.
Critical Limitations: The framework was evaluated on offline benchmark datasets and lacks validation on real-time traffic streams, encrypted communications, and resource-constrained edge devices. The study also does not evaluate energy consumption, deployment scalability, or healthcare-specific communication protocols.
Future Directions: Future work should investigate encrypted traffic analysis, real-time deployment, hardware-aware optimization, parameter quantization, edge computing integration, and validation within healthcare-specific IoMT environments.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it demonstrates the effectiveness of combining multiple machine learning and deep learning classifiers through metaheuristic optimization. The study provides a strong blueprint for adaptive ensemble intrusion detection systems capable of maintaining high detection performance across heterogeneous network environments while improving robustness and classification stability.

Dataset: WUSTL-EHMS-2020 dataset containing 35 network traffic features and 8 patient biometric features collected from a real-time healthcare monitoring environment with normal and attack instances.
Used Methods: Kernel Principal Component Analysis (KPCA), Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE), Deep Neural Networks (Net1–Net5), StackMean, StackMax, StackRF, Deep Learning (DL), Ensemble Learning
XAI: No explicit SHAP, LIME, or post-hoc explainability framework; transparency is provided through documented ensemble aggregation mechanisms, probability pooling strategies, and feature-effect analyses associated with the preprocessing pipeline.
Core Methodology: Develops a hierarchical stacked deep learning framework that first applies KPCA for non-linear feature extraction and dimensionality reduction, followed by SMOTE for class balancing. Five independent neural networks are then trained, and their outputs are combined using three ensemble strategies: StackMean, StackMax, and StackRF, where Random Forest acts as a meta-learner for final decision fusion.
Major Findings: The stacked ensemble models consistently outperformed individual neural networks. StackMean achieved 94.29% accuracy and 75.61% F1-score on the original dataset, while SMOTE significantly improved minority-class detection and sensitivity, reaching 86.31% for StackMax. StackRF achieved the highest precision among the evaluated ensemble configurations.
Critical Limitations: The framework relies on centralized training, which conflicts with privacy-preserving healthcare requirements. While SMOTE improves recall and sensitivity, it also introduces additional false positives that slightly reduce precision. The computational complexity of training multiple deep networks may also limit deployment on resource-constrained devices.
Future Directions: Future research should focus on integrating stacked deep learning architectures into Federated Learning environments, developing lightweight ensemble variants for edge deployment, improving privacy preservation, and reducing computational overhead while maintaining detection performance.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it demonstrates how deep ensemble learning, non-linear feature extraction, and class-imbalance handling can be combined to improve intrusion detection performance in healthcare environments. The study provides a practical framework for integrating network traffic and patient biometric information within a multi-model IDS architecture.

Dataset: Three custom datasets generated from a physical Raspberry Pi testbed, including Local Detection Engine (LDE) behavioral data, Central Detection Engine (CDE) behavioral data, and CDE network traffic data representing realistic device behavior and cyberattack scenarios.
Used Methods: One-Class SVM (OCSVM), Local Outlier Factor (LOF), Isolation Forest (IsoForest), Minimum Covariance Determinant (MCD), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Gaussian Kernel Density Estimation (G_KDE), Parzen Window Kernel Density Estimation (PW_KDE), Bayesian Gaussian Mixture Models (B_GMM), Anomaly Detection, Novelty Detection
XAI: No explicit SHAP, LIME, or post-hoc explainability framework; transparency is achieved through probabilistic density estimation, explicit anomaly thresholds, statistical scoring mechanisms, and structured JSON-based alert reporting.
Core Methodology: Develops a hierarchical anomaly-based intrusion detection architecture consisting of a Local Detection Engine deployed on Raspberry Pi devices and a Central Detection Engine operating at the gateway layer. Host-level behavioral telemetry and network traffic are collected, normalized, and analyzed using multiple novelty and anomaly detection algorithms to identify malicious activities without requiring labeled attack data.
Major Findings: Kernel Density Estimation models (G_KDE and PW_KDE) achieved near-perfect classification performance with AUC values approaching 1.0 during offline evaluations. Runtime experiments using stress-ng and hping3 confirmed strong resilience against denial-of-service attacks while maintaining low computational overhead. The framework demonstrated that lightweight unsupervised anomaly detection can effectively protect resource-constrained devices.
Critical Limitations: Several density-based models exhibited performance degradation and overfitting tendencies when transitioning from offline datasets to dynamic real-world network environments. Scalability across large heterogeneous deployments and long-term operational robustness remain unverified.
Future Directions: Future work should investigate large-scale healthcare deployments, energy-consumption analysis, adaptive online retraining mechanisms, continual learning strategies, and automated responses to evolving zero-day attack behaviors.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Highly relevant to IoMT IDS research because it demonstrates that lightweight anomaly detection methods can provide effective protection without requiring expensive supervised deep learning models.
