XAI: Identifies explainability as an emerging requirement in IoT-enabled healthcare systems. The study highlights that as Artificial Intelligence and Deep Learning become increasingly integrated into healthcare IoT applications, the resulting black-box decision processes may hinder clinical trust, adoption, and regulatory acceptance, creating a growing need for explainable and transparent AI mechanisms.
Core Methodology: Provides a comprehensive bibliometric mapping of IoT-healthcare research: (1) Analyzes publication growth, collaboration patterns, and research productivity across countries, institutions, and authors; (2) Identifies major research themes through keyword co-occurrence networks including Blockchain, Artificial Intelligence, 5G, Cloud Computing, Security, Privacy, and Data Analytics; (3) Uses co-citation analysis to uncover influential knowledge clusters such as authentication mechanisms, fog computing, smart healthcare, and IoT security; and (4) Tracks the evolution of healthcare IoT research from basic monitoring systems toward intelligent, autonomous, and data-driven healthcare ecosystems.
Major Findings: • IoT-healthcare research has experienced rapid and continuous growth, indicating increasing global interest in connected healthcare systems. • Security, privacy, authentication, blockchain, artificial intelligence, and smart healthcare emerge as dominant research themes. • The field is progressively shifting from simple health monitoring toward intelligent healthcare systems capable of predictive analytics and autonomous decision support. • Research activity is geographically concentrated, with China, India, and Saudi Arabia contributing significantly to IoT-healthcare development. • Blockchain and AI are increasingly viewed as complementary technologies for addressing healthcare security and trust challenges.
Critical Limitations: • Existing literature remains dominated by narrative reviews rather than objective systematic or bibliometric evaluations. • Significant interoperability challenges persist due to heterogeneous devices, communication protocols, and vendor-specific ecosystems. • Many proposed healthcare IoT solutions remain proof-of-concept implementations with limited real-world scalability validation. • Security and privacy frameworks often evolve independently rather than being integrated into holistic healthcare architectures.
Future Directions: • Investigate deeper integration of Artificial Intelligence, Blockchain, and IoT to establish privacy-preserving healthcare ecosystems. • Develop standardized interoperability and security frameworks to support large-scale deployment. • Create benchmark datasets and evaluation standards to facilitate objective comparison of healthcare IoT solutions. • Promote real-world implementation studies that move beyond laboratory prototypes and isolated pilot deployments.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly advances IoMT IDS research by providing a high-level landscape analysis of the healthcare IoT ecosystem and identifying security, privacy, and authentication as dominant research priorities. The study demonstrates that future IoMT intrusion detection systems cannot operate as isolated security components; instead, they must integrate with complementary technologies such as Blockchain, Fog Computing, Artificial Intelligence, and Privacy-Preserving Architectures. It further highlights that interoperability, authentication, and secure data exchange remain fundamental challenges, positioning intelligent IDS frameworks as essential building blocks within broader IoMT security ecosystems.

Dataset: Large-scale passive monitoring dataset involving 40 Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) patients and proof-of-concept validation using 10 Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) patients, integrating Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM), insulin administration records, physical activity, heart rate, and sleep-related data collected through wearable IoMT devices.
Used Methods: Machine Learning (ML), Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Regression (SVR), Bayesian Regularized Neural Networks (BRNN), Personalized Predictive Analytics, Sliding Window Temporal Modeling.
XAI: Does not explicitly employ post-hoc Explainable AI frameworks such as SHAP or LIME. Interpretability is primarily achieved through clinically meaningful physiological variables and physician understanding of the relationships between glucose levels, insulin administration, heart rate, sleep quality, and physical activity patterns.
Core Methodology: Proposes a personalized short-term glucose prediction framework for diabetes management: (1) Collects multi-modal physiological and behavioral information from wearable IoMT devices; (2) Integrates CGM measurements, insulin intake, physical activity, heart rate, and sleep metrics into a unified predictive pipeline; (3) Applies Random Forest, Support Vector Regression, and Bayesian Regularized Neural Networks to forecast future glucose levels; and (4) Utilizes a six-hour Past Sliding Window (PSW) to capture the most informative temporal patterns for personalized glucose prediction.
Major Findings: • Random Forest achieved the best predictive performance, obtaining an average prediction error of 18.60 mg/dL for 30-minute forecasting horizons. • A six-hour historical observation window was identified as the optimal temporal context for glucose prediction, while longer windows introduced unnecessary noise and reduced accuracy. • Personalized IoMT-driven prediction significantly improves glycemic management compared with generic population-level approaches. • Multi-modal wearable sensing enables more accurate forecasting by capturing behavioral and physiological factors influencing glucose fluctuations.
Critical Limitations: • Prediction performance depends heavily on patient adherence to monitoring protocols and consistent wearable device usage. • Training and optimization introduce computational overhead that may challenge deployment on legacy or resource-constrained medical devices. • Validation remains limited in scale and requires broader population studies to assess generalizability across diverse demographic and clinical groups.
Future Directions: • Extend monitoring durations beyond fourteen days to evaluate long-term robustness and adaptation capabilities. • Deploy lightweight real-time prediction models directly on wearable or edge devices for immediate intervention support. • Investigate adaptive and personalized learning strategies capable of automatically adjusting to evolving patient behaviors and physiological changes. • Integrate predictive models with automated clinical alerting mechanisms for hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia prevention.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly advances IoMT IDS research by demonstrating the critical importance of protecting high-value physiological telemetry streams used for automated medical decision-making. Since continuous glucose measurements, heart rate signals, insulin records, and activity data directly influence therapeutic recommendations and potentially insulin dosing decisions, any sensor spoofing, data injection, manipulation, replay attack, or telemetry corruption could lead to dangerous clinical outcomes. The study provides strong justification for developing lightweight, real-time IoMT intrusion detection systems capable of ensuring the integrity, authenticity, and availability of continuous healthcare telemetry throughout the entire sensing, transmission, and decision-support pipeline.

Dataset: Comprehensive review of spatial-temporal datasets and Cyber-Physical System (CPS) applications spanning healthcare, transportation, manufacturing, and industrial monitoring environments, focusing on datasets used for anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, and intelligent decision-making.
Used Methods: Deep Learning (DL), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), Spatial-Temporal Modeling, Anomaly Detection, Predictive Maintenance.
XAI: Identifies Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) as an emerging and essential research direction for Cyber-Physical Systems. The study emphasizes that highly complex deep learning architectures often operate as black boxes, making it difficult for operators to understand anomaly detection decisions, predictive maintenance alerts, and automated system responses.
Core Methodology: Proposes a three-dimensional taxonomy for Deep Learning in Cyber-Physical Systems: (1) CPS Domain Layer covering transportation systems, manufacturing systems, healthcare systems, and smart infrastructures; (2) Task Layer including spatial-temporal processing, anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, real-time decision-making, and multi-modal data fusion; and (3) Deep Learning Layer incorporating CNNs for spatial feature extraction, RNN/LSTM architectures for temporal dependency modeling, and GNNs for capturing complex graph-based relationships among interconnected CPS components.
Major Findings: • Deep learning architectures significantly outperform conventional statistical approaches when modeling complex spatial-temporal CPS behaviors. • CNNs effectively capture spatial dependencies, while RNNs and LSTMs excel at learning temporal dynamics in sequential CPS data streams. • Graph Neural Networks provide superior capability for analyzing interconnected CPS environments by modeling non-Euclidean relationships among system entities. • Anomaly detection and predictive maintenance emerge as the most impactful CPS applications, enabling proactive identification of faults and abnormal behaviors before system failure occurs.
Critical Limitations: • Advanced hybrid architectures such as CNN-LSTM and GNN-RNN require large-scale training datasets and substantial computational resources. • Resource-intensive training and inference processes can conflict with strict real-time operational requirements of CPS environments. • Security robustness against adversarial manipulation and AI-targeted attacks remains insufficiently investigated. • Limited availability of high-quality labeled CPS datasets creates challenges for model generalization and deployment.
Future Directions: • Developing lightweight and computationally efficient deep learning architectures suitable for edge deployment. • Addressing data scarcity and cold-start challenges through advanced transfer learning and self-supervised learning strategies. • Improving data quality assurance mechanisms for CPS environments. • Investigating adversarial resilience and security hardening techniques for deep learning-driven CPS anomaly detection systems. • Advancing Explainable AI frameworks that provide transparent reasoning for anomaly detection and predictive maintenance decisions.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly advances IoMT IDS research by providing a comprehensive framework for modeling spatial-temporal relationships within medical Cyber-Physical Systems. The study demonstrates how advanced deep learning architectures can move beyond static rule-based intrusion detection by learning complex interactions among physiological sensors, medical devices, communication networks, and healthcare infrastructure. It provides a strong foundation for designing next-generation IoMT IDS frameworks capable of detecting sophisticated multi-stage attacks, sensor manipulation attempts, abnormal behavioral patterns, and cyber-physical anomalies within interconnected healthcare ecosystems.

Dataset: Comprehensive survey of Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) literature, healthcare architectures, security frameworks, privacy-preserving technologies, and intelligent healthcare monitoring systems across modern medical ecosystems.
Used Methods: Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), Supervised Learning, Unsupervised Learning, Reinforcement Learning, Blockchain, Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), Zero-Trust Security, Encryption Technologies, Healthcare Data Analytics.
XAI: Does not explicitly implement Explainable AI frameworks such as SHAP or LIME; however, the study implicitly highlights explainability as a critical requirement for trustworthy AI-driven healthcare systems where clinicians must understand and validate automated recommendations before adoption in real-world medical environments.
Core Methodology: Presents a holistic framework describing the evolution of IoMT ecosystems: (1) Analyzes the transition from traditional healthcare infrastructures toward automated, cloud-connected, and intelligent healthcare systems; (2) Examines the integration of Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Reinforcement Learning into healthcare monitoring, diagnostics, and predictive analytics; (3) Evaluates major cybersecurity threats targeting IoMT environments including malware, denial-of-service attacks, unauthorized access, and device manipulation; and (4) Reviews existing security mechanisms such as encryption, blockchain, trusted execution environments, and zero-trust architectures for protecting healthcare infrastructures.
Major Findings: • The evolution of IoMT significantly improves healthcare efficiency, remote monitoring capabilities, and predictive clinical decision-making through real-time data collection and intelligent analytics. • Machine Learning and Deep Learning technologies play a transformative role in diagnosis, patient monitoring, and healthcare prediction but simultaneously introduce new attack vectors such as adversarial manipulation and data poisoning. • Security and privacy are foundational requirements for sustainable IoMT adoption and regulatory compliance rather than optional technical enhancements. • Emerging technologies such as blockchain, zero-trust architectures, and trusted execution environments offer promising solutions for strengthening healthcare cybersecurity resilience.
Critical Limitations: • Strong security mechanisms often introduce significant computational, communication, and energy overheads that exceed the capabilities of many resource-constrained medical devices. • The absence of standardized security frameworks across manufacturers creates interoperability and deployment challenges. • Legacy medical devices frequently lack sufficient processing resources to support advanced cryptographic and security mechanisms. • Balancing security, privacy, usability, and real-time performance remains a persistent challenge across IoMT deployments.
Future Directions: • Develop lightweight, energy-efficient security and cryptographic protocols specifically optimized for constrained IoMT devices. • Expand adoption of zero-trust security architectures to minimize trust assumptions across healthcare networks. • Investigate decentralized blockchain-enabled security models capable of reducing single points of failure. • Design standardized security frameworks that facilitate interoperability among heterogeneous medical devices and healthcare infrastructures. • Advance trustworthy and explainable AI technologies that support secure and transparent healthcare decision-making.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly advances IoMT IDS research by providing a comprehensive security-oriented view of the modern IoMT attack surface. The study identifies denial-of-service attacks, malware propagation, unauthorized access, and device manipulation as major threats while emphasizing the critical role of intrusion detection systems in protecting continuous healthcare monitoring environments. It highlights that future IoMT IDS frameworks must be lightweight, hardware-aware, energy-efficient, and capable of operating alongside complementary security technologies such as blockchain, zero-trust architectures, and trusted execution environments to provide effective protection across heterogeneous healthcare ecosystems.

Dataset: Evaluated using three publicly available Chest X-ray (CXR) datasets comprising 13,757 images covering COVID-19, Pneumonia, Tuberculosis (TB), and healthy subjects for multi-disease pulmonary abnormality classification.
Used Methods: Deep Learning (DL), Lightweight Deep Neural Network (DNN), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Transfer Learning, Medical Image Classification, Computer-Aided Diagnosis (CADx), 10-Fold Cross Validation.
XAI: Does not explicitly implement formal Explainable AI frameworks such as SHAP or LIME; however, the study emphasizes the importance of computer-aided diagnosis systems that can support clinicians and radiologists in making transparent and trustworthy diagnostic decisions within healthcare environments.
Core Methodology: Proposes a lightweight deep learning framework for pulmonary disease diagnosis: (1) Performs image preprocessing through grayscale conversion and resizing to 224×224 pixels; (2) Utilizes a compact deep neural architecture consisting of convolutional, max-pooling, dropout, and fully connected layers; (3) Conducts multi-class disease classification across COVID-19, Pneumonia, Tuberculosis, and healthy categories; and (4) Benchmarks performance against larger state-of-the-art architectures including ResNet and Inception-based models while maintaining significantly lower computational complexity.
Major Findings: • Achieved exceptionally high classification performance with accuracies of 99.87% for COVID-19 detection, 99.55% for Pneumonia detection, and 99.76% for Tuberculosis detection. • The lightweight architecture outperformed several larger state-of-the-art deep learning models despite requiring substantially fewer parameters and computational resources. • Demonstrates that efficient deep learning architectures can achieve clinical-grade diagnostic performance without relying on computationally expensive models. • The compact design makes deployment feasible in resource-constrained healthcare environments where processing power and energy availability are limited.
Critical Limitations: • Performance comparisons may be influenced by differences in dataset composition, image quality, and class distributions across benchmark datasets. • The study lacks extensive external validation across diverse demographic populations and healthcare institutions. • Potential risks of dataset bias and limited generalizability remain insufficiently explored. • Real-world deployment challenges, including heterogeneous imaging devices and clinical workflow integration, are not extensively evaluated.
Future Directions: • Validate model performance using larger multi-center and cross-population datasets to improve generalization. • Investigate federated learning frameworks that enable collaborative hospital training while preserving patient privacy. • Develop explainable diagnostic mechanisms to improve clinician trust and model transparency. • Extend lightweight architectures toward real-time deployment on edge healthcare devices and mobile diagnostic platforms.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly informs IoMT IDS research by demonstrating how highly efficient lightweight deep learning architectures can deliver near state-of-the-art performance while operating under strict computational constraints. The study provides a valuable blueprint for designing edge-enabled intrusion detection systems that must run on resource-constrained medical devices, gateways, and wearable sensors. Its emphasis on low-complexity yet high-performance deep learning aligns closely with future IoMT IDS requirements where rapid anomaly detection, minimal latency, reduced energy consumption, and deployment feasibility on constrained healthcare hardware are critical operational objectives.

Dataset: Evaluated through a large-scale international digital experiment involving 389 board-certified dermatologists and 459 primary-care physicians from 39 countries who assessed 364 dermatological images covering 46 distinct skin diseases across diverse skin-tone groups.
Used Methods: Artificial Intelligence (AI), Clinical Decision Support Systems, Human-AI Collaboration, Diagnostic Performance Evaluation, Teledermatology, Bias Analysis, Healthcare Analytics.
XAI: Focuses on the practical impact of AI-assisted decision support rather than formal Explainable AI frameworks. The study evaluates how algorithmic accuracy, fairness, and inclusiveness influence physician performance and demonstrates that trustworthy AI systems must provide equitable support across diverse patient populations to avoid amplifying existing healthcare disparities.
Core Methodology: Investigates physician-AI collaboration within teledermatology environments: (1) Conducts a randomized digital diagnostic experiment using dermatological images; (2) Compares physician diagnostic performance with and without AI assistance; (3) Evaluates the influence of algorithmic accuracy and fairness on clinical outcomes; and (4) Examines performance disparities across different skin-tone populations to determine whether AI systems reduce or worsen diagnostic inequities.
Major Findings: • Physicians demonstrated approximately 4% lower diagnostic accuracy when evaluating darker skin tones compared with lighter skin tones. • AI-assisted decision support can significantly improve physician diagnostic performance when the underlying AI model is accurate and unbiased. • Algorithmic bias can reinforce existing healthcare inequalities if fairness considerations are not incorporated during model development. • Human-AI collaboration is most effective when AI systems complement physician expertise rather than replace clinical judgement. • Inclusive and representative AI models are essential for achieving equitable healthcare outcomes across diverse patient populations.
Critical Limitations: • The study relies on a store-and-forward teledermatology simulation, which may not perfectly reflect real-world clinical environments. • Physician behavior within controlled experiments may differ from decision-making under actual clinical pressure. • The work focuses on diagnostic support rather than broader healthcare operational systems. • Results remain dependent on the quality and representativeness of the datasets used to train AI models.
Future Directions: • Develop fairness-aware AI systems that explicitly address performance disparities across demographic groups. • Investigate human-AI interaction mechanisms that improve collaboration without introducing cognitive bias. • Expand evaluation frameworks to assess fairness, trustworthiness, and inclusiveness alongside predictive performance. • Develop more representative datasets that accurately reflect diverse patient populations and clinical scenarios.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly informs IoMT IDS research by highlighting the critical importance of fairness, bias mitigation, and trustworthy AI in security-critical healthcare environments. Just as biased diagnostic systems can underperform for specific patient groups, biased intrusion detection systems may underperform for specific device types, patient populations, communication protocols, or hospital environments. The study demonstrates that future IoMT IDS frameworks should evaluate not only accuracy and detection rates but also fairness, robustness, and equitable protection across heterogeneous medical devices to ensure that no subset of healthcare infrastructure becomes disproportionately vulnerable to cyber threats.

Dataset: Evaluated using longitudinal Parkinson’s Disease (PD) monitoring data collected through multiple research initiatives including MoMoPa, HELP, REMPARK, PARK-IT2, and real-world home monitoring studies involving patients with motor fluctuations.
Used Methods: Machine Learning (ML), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Epsilon-Support Vector Regression (ε-SVR), Wearable Computing, Activity Recognition, Clinical Monitoring, Time-Series Analysis.
XAI: Does not explicitly implement formal Explainable AI frameworks such as SHAP or LIME. Instead, interpretability is achieved through clinically meaningful symptom reports and objective motor-state indicators that neurologists can directly understand and use for treatment decisions, reducing reliance on subjective patient diaries.
Core Methodology: Introduces the STAT-ON™ wearable medical monitoring system: (1) Utilizes a waist-mounted inertial sensor to continuously collect movement and gait information; (2) Applies self-adaptive machine learning algorithms including SVM and ε-SVR to identify Parkinson’s motor states; (3) Detects clinically significant events such as ON/OFF fluctuations, dyskinesia, and Freezing of Gait (FoG); and (4) Generates objective, real-time reports that support neurologists in treatment optimization and long-term disease management.
Major Findings: • STAT-ON™ provides significantly more objective and reliable monitoring than traditional patient diaries and subjective clinical assessments. • Demonstrates high usability and acceptance among patients, caregivers, and neurologists, with satisfaction scores exceeding 8/10 in real-world deployments. • Successfully detects motor fluctuations, dyskinesia episodes, and gait disturbances under uncontrolled daily-life conditions. • Continuous wearable monitoring improves clinical visibility into disease progression and supports more personalized treatment strategies. • The system demonstrates the practical viability of AI-driven wearable monitoring in home healthcare environments.
Critical Limitations: • The ON/OFF fluctuation detection model requires approximately three days of patient-specific learning before achieving optimal performance. • Validation has primarily focused on mid-to-advanced Parkinson’s Disease patients, limiting evidence for early-stage disease monitoring. • Performance may be reduced for patients with severe mobility impairments who cannot generate sufficient gait-related signals. • The framework currently focuses primarily on motor symptoms and provides limited coverage of non-motor manifestations of Parkinson’s Disease.
Future Directions: • Extend validation studies to early-stage Parkinson’s Disease populations. • Develop closed-loop therapeutic systems capable of automatically adapting treatment strategies based on detected symptoms. • Integrate monitoring of non-motor symptoms such as sleep disorders, depression, and cognitive decline. • Enhance adaptive learning mechanisms to reduce calibration periods and improve personalization efficiency.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly advances IoMT IDS research by demonstrating the importance of context-aware anomaly detection in healthcare environments. The study highlights that not all abnormal physiological patterns represent cyberattacks; many reflect legitimate clinical conditions. Future IoMT IDS frameworks must therefore distinguish between genuine patient deterioration, disease-related physiological anomalies, sensor malfunctions, and malicious data manipulation attempts. This paper provides a strong foundation for developing clinically aware IDS architectures that minimize false alarms while maintaining patient safety in continuous remote monitoring systems.

Dataset: Systematic review of wearable sensor studies, clinical atrial fibrillation (AF) screening research, and artificial intelligence-based diagnostic benchmarks involving ECG and PPG monitoring technologies.
Used Methods: Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), Electrocardiography (ECG), Photoplethysmography (PPG), Wearable Health Monitoring.
XAI: Highlights the importance of explainable and clinically interpretable AI systems for healthcare adoption. The study emphasizes that AI-generated diagnostic outputs must be understandable and justifiable to clinicians before they can be trusted in routine patient care and therapeutic decision-making processes.
Core Methodology: Provides a comprehensive review of AI-enabled wearable technologies for atrial fibrillation detection: (1) Categorizes wearable monitoring platforms into ECG-based and PPG-based systems; (2) Reviews machine learning and deep learning approaches, including CNN and RNN architectures, for rhythm classification and AF detection; (3) Evaluates diagnostic performance across consumer-grade and medical-grade wearable devices; and (4) Examines how wearable-generated telemetry can be integrated into clinical workflows for large-scale cardiovascular screening and early intervention.
Major Findings: • AI-powered wearable devices provide scalable, non-invasive, and continuous atrial fibrillation screening capabilities that outperform traditional episodic clinical monitoring. • Deep learning architectures, particularly CNN-based models, achieve high sensitivity and specificity when identifying abnormal cardiac rhythms from wearable telemetry streams. • Continuous wearable monitoring supports earlier AF detection, enabling timely clinical intervention and potentially reducing stroke incidence. • Combining AI analytics with wearable technologies creates a viable pathway toward population-scale cardiovascular monitoring and preventive healthcare. • Wearable-based monitoring significantly improves access to long-term cardiac surveillance outside traditional healthcare facilities.
Critical Limitations: • Wearable sensor data is highly susceptible to motion artifacts, signal distortion, and environmental noise that may negatively impact AI diagnostic performance. • Clinical adoption is constrained by the lack of standardized protocols for interpreting, validating, and responding to AI-generated alerts. • Significant variation exists among commercial wearable platforms regarding sensor quality and diagnostic reliability. • Regulatory and interoperability challenges continue to hinder large-scale integration into routine healthcare practice.
Future Directions: • Develop advanced on-device signal processing techniques to improve robustness against motion artifacts and noisy environments. • Establish standardized clinical workflows and vendor-neutral protocols for AI-assisted AF screening and alert management. • Improve interoperability among wearable devices, healthcare platforms, and electronic health record systems. • Advance real-time edge-based analytics capable of performing accurate cardiovascular assessment directly on wearable hardware.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly advances IoMT IDS research by emphasizing the security importance of wearable-generated clinical telemetry. Since diagnostic decisions increasingly depend on continuous ECG and PPG streams, future IoMT IDS frameworks must protect against sensor spoofing, signal manipulation, data poisoning, and telemetry integrity attacks that could produce false arrhythmia diagnoses or conceal genuine cardiac events. The study highlights the need for security architectures that simultaneously verify device authenticity, data integrity, signal reliability, and network trustworthiness across wearable healthcare ecosystems.

Dataset: Evaluated using the Stress-Lysis.csv dataset containing 2,001 physiological records consisting of body temperature, humidity (sweat level), step counts, and associated stress classifications (low, normal, and high stress levels).
Used Methods: Machine Learning (ML), Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting (GB), Stacked Ensemble Method (SEM), Logistic Regression, Wearable Computing, Physiological Signal Analytics.
XAI: Does not explicitly implement Explainable AI techniques such as SHAP or LIME. Interpretability is implicitly derived from the physiological variables used for classification, where temperature, sweat response, and movement patterns are directly associated with stress-related physiological states.
Core Methodology: Proposes the Stress-Track intelligent stress monitoring framework: (1) Collects physiological signals including body temperature, humidity/sweat measurements, and physical activity information through wearable wristband sensors; (2) Securely transmits sensor telemetry via Wi-Fi infrastructure to cloud-based services; (3) Applies a stacked ensemble architecture combining Random Forest and Gradient Boosting models; and (4) Utilizes a Logistic Regression meta-learner to classify stress levels into low, normal, and high-risk categories with enhanced predictive reliability.
Major Findings: • The proposed Stress-Track framework achieved 99.5% classification accuracy, demonstrating exceptional performance in physiological stress assessment. • The stacked ensemble architecture outperformed individual machine learning models by leveraging complementary strengths from Random Forest and Gradient Boosting algorithms. • Multi-modal physiological sensing (temperature, sweat, and activity data) provided significantly richer predictive capability than single-sensor approaches. • The model achieved an AUC score of 0.95, confirming strong discriminative power and classification robustness. • Demonstrates the feasibility of real-time wearable health analytics through cloud-connected IoMT infrastructures.
Critical Limitations: • Large-scale deployment remains challenging due to device heterogeneity, communication variability, and infrastructure scalability constraints. • Data privacy, regulatory compliance, and secure handling of sensitive physiological information require deeper investigation. • Performance has primarily been validated on a controlled dataset rather than highly diverse real-world healthcare environments. • Interoperability challenges may arise when integrating different wearable hardware platforms and communication protocols.
Future Directions: • Develop stronger privacy-preserving mechanisms for sensitive physiological data protection. • Investigate scalable deployment across heterogeneous wearable ecosystems and healthcare infrastructures. • Explore interoperability standards that support seamless integration among diverse IoMT devices. • Extend validation studies using larger populations and real-world clinical monitoring environments.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly informs IoMT IDS research by emphasizing the importance of protecting physiological telemetry streams transmitted by wearable healthcare systems. Because automated stress assessments depend on temperature, sweat, and activity measurements, malicious manipulation of these signals could trigger incorrect clinical interpretations or behavioral interventions. The study highlights the need for IoMT IDS frameworks capable of verifying sensor authenticity, protecting telemetry integrity, securing wireless communication channels, and detecting abnormal physiological data patterns resulting from spoofing, injection, or tampering attacks.

Dataset: Systematic review of Ambient Assisted Living (AAL), cardiovascular disease (CVD) management systems, wearable healthcare technologies, telemedicine platforms, and IoT-enabled self-monitoring solutions for aging populations.
Used Methods: Systematic Literature Review (SLR), PRISMA Methodology, Ambient Assisted Living (AAL), Internet of Things (IoT), Mobile Health (mHealth), Telemedicine, Remote Patient Monitoring (RPM), Cardiovascular Self-Management Systems.
XAI: Does not explicitly implement Explainable AI techniques such as SHAP or LIME. However, the study emphasizes that AAL systems must provide transparent, understandable, and actionable health information to improve patient engagement, encourage self-management, and maintain trust among elderly users and healthcare providers.
Core Methodology: Provides a comprehensive review of Ambient Assisted Living solutions for cardiovascular disease management: (1) Examines wearable and self-monitoring technologies used for continuous cardiovascular assessment; (2) Reviews AAL frameworks designed to support aging populations in home-based environments; (3) Evaluates clinician-facing monitoring and decision-support systems; and (4) Analyzes the integration of IoT, mHealth, telemedicine, and remote monitoring technologies to improve cardiovascular self-management, reduce hospital admissions, and enhance quality of life.
Major Findings: • Ambient Assisted Living systems significantly improve cardiovascular self-management and support aging populations in maintaining independence. • Continuous wearable monitoring enables proactive healthcare interventions by identifying cardiovascular deterioration before critical events occur. • Integration of IoT, telemedicine, and mHealth platforms improves patient engagement, treatment adherence, and communication between patients and healthcare providers. • AAL environments reduce pressure on healthcare facilities by enabling remote supervision and long-term disease management. • Remote monitoring technologies support a transition from reactive healthcare toward proactive and preventive care models.
Critical Limitations: • Elderly populations often face usability challenges due to device complexity, maintenance requirements, and technology adoption barriers. • Lack of standardized interoperability frameworks complicates integration between heterogeneous sensors, monitoring platforms, and healthcare information systems. • Security and privacy concerns remain significant due to the continuous collection and transmission of highly sensitive health data. • Large-scale deployment remains challenging because of varying device standards and communication protocols.
Future Directions: • Develop intuitive and user-friendly interfaces tailored specifically for elderly users. • Establish standardized interoperability protocols that support seamless communication across diverse healthcare platforms and sensor ecosystems. • Improve privacy-preserving communication and data-sharing mechanisms for long-term remote monitoring. • Expand AAL systems through scalable and secure IoMT infrastructures capable of supporting larger patient populations.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly advances IoMT IDS research by highlighting the unique security requirements of Ambient Assisted Living environments. Since AAL systems continuously collect and transmit highly sensitive cardiovascular information from vulnerable elderly populations, future IoMT IDS frameworks must provide strong privacy protection, low-latency monitoring, interoperability-aware security, and reliable anomaly detection without disrupting life-critical alerts. The study emphasizes that security mechanisms in healthcare must remain unobtrusive, lightweight, and patient-centered while safeguarding continuous medical telemetry against unauthorized access, manipulation, and privacy breaches.

Dataset: Multiple benchmark intrusion detection datasets including MQTT2020, CIDDS-001, UNSW-NB15, KDD++, NSL-KDD, and WSN-DS, covering wireless sensor network traffic, IoT communications, and cyberattack scenarios relevant to healthcare environments.
Used Methods: Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), Wireless Sensor Networks (WSN).
XAI: Does not explicitly employ Explainable AI frameworks such as SHAP or LIME. However, the study emphasizes the importance of interpretable, reliable, and clinically trustworthy IDS models that enable timely security decision-making and efficient threat mitigation within resource-constrained healthcare environments.
Core Methodology: Provides a comprehensive security review of Wireless Sensor Networks in IoMT environments: (1) Classifies WSN architectures including layered, clustered, and hybrid deployments; (2) Examines network topologies such as star, mesh, and hybrid configurations; (3) Categorizes cyberattacks including Passive Attacks, Active Attacks, DoS, Sybil, Sinkhole, Grayhole, Replay, and Routing Attacks; and (4) Maps machine learning and deep learning intrusion detection techniques to specific attack categories and network vulnerabilities.
Major Findings: • Wireless Sensor Networks represent one of the most vulnerable components of IoMT infrastructures due to limited computational power, battery constraints, and open wireless communication channels. • Deep Learning approaches, particularly hybrid CNN-LSTM models, achieve superior attack classification performance (up to 96.02%) compared to traditional machine learning methods (approximately 91%). • Effective IoMT security requires balancing detection accuracy, computational efficiency, energy consumption, and communication overhead. • Multi-layer IDS frameworks provide stronger protection than isolated security mechanisms by detecting attacks across different protocol layers.
Critical Limitations: • Many evaluated studies rely heavily on synthetic, laboratory-generated, or small-scale benchmark datasets that may not accurately represent real-world healthcare traffic characteristics. • High false-positive rates remain a major operational challenge and can contribute to alert fatigue among healthcare administrators. • Resource limitations of sensor nodes restrict the deployment of computationally intensive deep learning architectures.
Future Directions: • Develop lightweight and energy-efficient IDS frameworks optimized for low-power wireless medical sensors. • Validate IDS performance using large-scale, real-world heterogeneous IoMT datasets collected from operational healthcare environments. • Integrate proactive defense mechanisms and intrusion-tolerant architectures alongside traditional reactive detection systems. • Improve model generalization and reduce false-positive rates for practical clinical deployment.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly advances IoMT IDS research by providing one of the most comprehensive taxonomies of Wireless Sensor Network threats within healthcare environments. The study demonstrates that future IoMT IDS architectures must operate across multiple protocol layers and simultaneously defend against physical-layer attacks, routing manipulation, wireless communication threats, and application-layer intrusions. Its emphasis on lightweight, accurate, and resource-aware detection aligns closely with the practical requirements of securing large-scale Remote Patient Monitoring and IoMT ecosystems.

Dataset: Large-scale streaming cardiovascular telemetry collected from wearable medical devices, focusing on real-time monitoring of COVID-19 patients with cardiovascular comorbidities through 5G-enabled healthcare infrastructures.
Used Methods: Deep Learning (DL), Edge Computing, 5G Communication Networks, Collaborative Neural Networks, Real-Time Health Monitoring, Wearable Medical Devices, Streaming Data Analytics.
XAI: Does not explicitly implement Explainable AI techniques such as SHAP or LIME. However, the framework emphasizes automated diagnostic support and intelligent alert generation to reduce physician workload and improve timely clinical decision-making in high-volume monitoring environments.
Core Methodology: Proposes a 5G-enabled real-time cardiovascular monitoring framework: (1) Collects continuous physiological data from wearable medical devices; (2) Utilizes edge computing infrastructure to process streaming health data close to the data source; (3) Employs collaborative deep learning models to distribute computational workloads across edge and cloud resources; and (4) Leverages ultra-low-latency 5G communication to support rapid transmission and analysis of life-critical cardiovascular telemetry.
Major Findings: • 5G-enabled healthcare architectures substantially reduce communication latency, enabling real-time monitoring and intervention for high-risk cardiovascular patients. • Collaborative neural network architectures efficiently distribute processing workloads across edge and cloud environments, improving scalability and computational efficiency. • Automated diagnostic pipelines reduce physician workload while enabling faster clinical response to deteriorating patient conditions. • Edge computing minimizes delays associated with centralized cloud processing and improves responsiveness for critical healthcare applications.
Critical Limitations: • Dependence on 5G infrastructure limits deployment in regions with insufficient network coverage or connectivity limitations. • Continuous generation of large-scale physiological data introduces substantial challenges related to storage, privacy preservation, and long-term data management. • High-volume streaming environments increase the complexity of maintaining secure and resilient healthcare communication infrastructures.
Future Directions: • Extend the framework to support additional chronic diseases and multimorbidity monitoring beyond cardiovascular conditions. • Develop stronger privacy-preserving mechanisms and secure communication protocols for healthcare data transmitted across 5G networks. • Improve scalability and long-term management of large-scale medical telemetry streams. • Investigate advanced edge-based intelligence capable of performing more autonomous healthcare analytics.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly advances IoMT IDS research by highlighting the emerging security challenges associated with 5G-enabled healthcare ecosystems. The study demonstrates that future IoMT intrusion detection systems must operate efficiently within edge-computing environments, analyze high-velocity streaming telemetry in real time, and detect anomalies without introducing latency that could jeopardize patient safety. It provides a strong architectural foundation for developing ultra-low-latency IDS frameworks designed specifically for next-generation 5G healthcare networks.

Dataset: Patient medical record datasets containing chronic disease information, specifically heart disease, diabetes, and stroke cases, including incomplete and heterogeneous clinical records requiring preprocessing and feature optimization.
Used Methods: Deep Auto-Encoder Model (DAEM), Golden Flower Search (GFS), Collaborative Bias Integrated Generative Adversarial Network (ColBGaN), Deep Learning (DL), Feature Selection, Data Imputation, Chronic Disease Classification.
XAI: Does not explicitly employ Explainable AI techniques such as SHAP or LIME. The framework primarily focuses on improving diagnostic accuracy and automated disease recognition through advanced preprocessing, feature optimization, and collaborative deep learning mechanisms.
Core Methodology: Proposes the DACL framework for chronic disease diagnosis: (1) Utilizes a Deep Auto-Encoder Model (DAEM) to handle missing values and improve medical data quality; (2) Applies Golden Flower Search (GFS) optimization to identify the most informative clinical features; (3) Employs a Collaborative Bias Integrated GAN (ColBGaN) to perform high-precision disease classification; and (4) Integrates preprocessing, feature optimization, and classification into a unified intelligent healthcare analytics pipeline.
Major Findings: • The DACL framework significantly improves chronic disease diagnosis by effectively addressing missing and incomplete medical records. • DAEM enhances data quality through intelligent imputation, improving downstream learning performance. • GFS accelerates model training and improves classification efficiency by selecting optimal feature subsets. • ColBGaN demonstrates strong capability for distinguishing among multiple chronic diseases including heart disease, diabetes, and stroke. • The integrated architecture provides a highly automated clinical decision-support workflow capable of improving diagnostic precision.
Critical Limitations: • Performance remains highly dependent on the quality, diversity, and completeness of the original clinical records. • The ColBGaN architecture introduces substantial computational complexity and may require powerful computing infrastructure. • Generalization across diverse healthcare populations remains insufficiently validated. • Deployment on low-resource healthcare edge environments may be challenging without model optimization.
Future Directions: • Validate the framework on larger and more diverse healthcare datasets to improve robustness and generalizability. • Optimize ColBGaN and related deep learning components for deployment on lightweight edge-based healthcare systems. • Investigate privacy-preserving collaborative learning approaches to support distributed healthcare analytics. • Extend the framework to support broader disease categories and multimodal clinical data sources.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly informs IoMT IDS research by demonstrating the importance of data quality preservation, intelligent feature optimization, and collaborative learning in healthcare environments. The study highlights that future IoMT IDS frameworks must not only detect malicious activity but also maintain the integrity of medical records against data tampering, corruption, missing-value attacks, and noise injection. The use of data imputation and feature optimization techniques provides valuable insight into how IDS systems can remain resilient when operating in imperfect or compromised healthcare data environments.

Dataset: Wearable sensor data collected from Fitbit wristbands in a clinical study involving patients recovering from pancreatic surgery, focusing on post-operative recovery monitoring, complication prediction, and hospital readmission risk assessment.
Used Methods: Multi-Level Feature Engineering, Singular Spectrum Analysis (SSA), Time-Series Analytics, Clinical Predictive Modeling, Wearable Health Monitoring, Post-Operative Risk Prediction.
XAI: Does not explicitly implement Explainable AI methods such as SHAP or LIME. However, the framework emphasizes transparent feature engineering, enabling clinicians to understand which physiological patterns contribute to complication prediction and recovery assessment.
Core Methodology: Proposes a wearable-driven clinical predictive analytics framework: (1) Collects noisy, incomplete, and fine-grained physiological time-series data from Fitbit devices; (2) Applies Singular Spectrum Analysis (SSA) and a multi-level feature engineering pipeline to extract meaningful physiological indicators from raw signals; (3) Generates high-level predictive features associated with patient recovery trajectories; and (4) Develops predictive models capable of identifying post-operative complications and hospital readmission risks before traditional clinical observation methods.
Major Findings: • Multi-level feature engineering significantly improves predictive performance compared to using raw wearable sensor signals alone. • Singular Spectrum Analysis effectively reduces noise and enhances the extraction of clinically meaningful physiological patterns. • Wearable monitoring enables early identification of post-operative complications outside traditional hospital environments, supporting proactive intervention. • The framework demonstrates that continuous wearable telemetry can serve as a reliable source of predictive healthcare intelligence when properly processed and engineered.
Critical Limitations: • Performance depends heavily on patient adherence and consistent wearable device usage throughout the monitoring period. • The study focuses on pancreatic surgery patients, limiting immediate generalizability to other surgical procedures or healthcare populations. • Variations in data completeness and sensor quality may influence prediction reliability. • Additional validation is required across broader clinical cohorts and healthcare settings.
Future Directions: • Evaluate the framework across multiple surgical specialties and larger patient populations. • Integrate real-time alerting systems capable of automatically notifying clinicians about emerging complication risks. • Develop scalable architectures capable of supporting continuous wearable monitoring at population scale. • Investigate advanced AI models that can further improve predictive performance while maintaining clinical interpretability.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly informs IoMT IDS research by demonstrating that the security of healthcare systems extends beyond raw sensor protection to feature integrity protection. Since clinical decisions rely on complex engineered features extracted from physiological telemetry, future IoMT IDS frameworks must protect not only the original sensor data but also the derived features used by predictive models. This highlights the need for feature-aware IDS architectures capable of detecting signal manipulation, feature poisoning, data injection, and telemetry corruption that could trigger false complication alerts or conceal genuine medical emergencies.

Dataset: Wearable Medical Sensor (WMS) data streams collected from resource-constrained healthcare edge devices supporting continuous disease monitoring and sequential health analytics tasks.
Used Methods: Deep Neural Network (DNN), Continual Learning (CL), Multi-Head Neural Networks, Data Preservation (DP), Synthetic Data Generation (SDG), Edge AI, Sequential Learning, Multi-Disease Detection.
XAI: Does not explicitly implement Explainable AI methods such as SHAP or LIME. The study prioritizes continual adaptation, computational efficiency, and long-term model sustainability on edge healthcare devices by preventing catastrophic forgetting during sequential learning.
Core Methodology: Proposes the DOCTOR framework for continual healthcare intelligence: (1) Utilizes a multi-headed Deep Neural Network architecture to support multiple disease detection tasks; (2) Implements Continual Learning mechanisms allowing the model to learn new disease categories sequentially without retraining from scratch; (3) Employs Data Preservation (DP) and Synthetic Data Generation (SDG) modules to retain prior knowledge and mitigate catastrophic forgetting; and (4) Optimizes memory consumption, battery usage, and computational overhead for deployment on resource-constrained wearable medical devices.
Major Findings: • DOCTOR enables wearable edge devices to continuously learn new disease detection tasks without requiring complete retraining. • Continual Learning significantly reduces storage requirements and computational costs compared with maintaining separate models for each disease. • Synthetic Data Generation effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting while preserving diagnostic performance across sequential tasks. • The framework demonstrates that adaptive healthcare AI can remain accurate while operating within the memory and battery constraints of wearable medical systems. • Supports sustainable long-term deployment of intelligent healthcare monitoring systems.
Critical Limitations: • Performance is strongly dependent on the quality and representativeness of synthetic data generated by the SDG component. • Balancing model expansion, memory consumption, battery usage, and detection performance remains challenging for highly constrained edge devices. • Sequential learning systems may still experience degradation when exposed to highly heterogeneous or rapidly evolving data distributions.
Future Directions: • Improve Synthetic Data Generation mechanisms to produce more realistic and representative training samples. • Extend continual learning capabilities beyond disease detection to broader healthcare applications including fitness monitoring, sleep assessment, and behavioral analytics. • Investigate more efficient memory-management strategies for ultra-low-power healthcare devices. • Evaluate continual learning under highly dynamic and heterogeneous real-world healthcare environments.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly advances IoMT IDS research by introducing a Continual Learning paradigm that can be adapted to cybersecurity applications. Similar to how DOCTOR sequentially learns new diseases without catastrophic forgetting, future IoMT intrusion detection systems could continuously learn emerging attack signatures, zero-day exploits, novel malware families, and evolving threat behaviors without requiring complete retraining. The framework provides a promising blueprint for adaptive IDS architectures capable of maintaining long-term effectiveness in dynamic healthcare cyber environments.

Dataset: Diverse clinical and ambient healthcare datasets focusing on elderly activity monitoring, fall detection, behavioral recognition, and Ambient Assisted Living (AAL) environments using multimodal sensor systems.
Used Methods: Deep Learning (DL), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Ambient Assisted Living (AAL), Activity Recognition, Fall Detection, Behavioral Analytics.

Major Findings: • Deep Learning models substantially outperform traditional threshold-based systems in elderly activity recognition and fall detection tasks. • Multimodal sensor fusion significantly improves monitoring robustness and behavioral classification accuracy in complex home-care environments. • Automated behavior recognition systems support independent living and enhance long-term elderly healthcare management. • Intelligent monitoring frameworks provide continuous safety supervision while reducing caregiver workload. • Ambient Assisted Living technologies demonstrate strong potential for proactive healthcare intervention and emergency response.
Critical Limitations: • Continuous monitoring through cameras and sensors raises significant privacy and ethical concerns regarding personal behavioral data collection. • Deep Learning models often require substantial computational resources that exceed the capabilities of many resource-constrained AAL edge devices. • Real-time deployment remains challenging due to energy consumption, processing requirements, and hardware limitations.
Future Directions: • Investigate privacy-preserving behavioral monitoring techniques including Federated Learning and privacy-aware analytics. • Develop lightweight and energy-efficient Deep Learning architectures suitable for edge-based AAL deployment. • Improve scalability and robustness across diverse elderly populations and home environments. • Explore adaptive monitoring systems capable of personalized behavioral modeling and anomaly detection.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly informs IoMT IDS research by highlighting the security requirements of Ambient Assisted Living ecosystems where highly sensitive behavioral and health-related data are continuously collected. The study demonstrates that future IoMT intrusion detection systems must be capable of distinguishing between genuine medical emergencies (such as falls or abnormal behavior patterns) and cybersecurity incidents. It further emphasizes that IDS mechanisms should operate with minimal latency and computational overhead to ensure that security controls never interfere with time-critical healthcare alerts, emergency response workflows, or patient safety operations within smart healthcare environments.

Dataset: Systematic survey of clinical literature, robot-assisted surgery datasets including Cholec80 and EndoVis, and technical benchmarks related to image-guided surgical robotics and computer-assisted intervention systems.
Used Methods: Deep Learning (DL), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN), Image Segmentation, Object Detection, Motion Tracking, Surgical Skill Assessment, Robot-Assisted Surgery (RAS).
XAI: Highlights the limitations of black-box Deep Learning models in safety-critical surgical environments and advocates for Explainable AI (XAI) frameworks capable of providing transparent and interpretable decision support for surgeons. The study emphasizes that trust and clinical adoption depend on understanding the rationale behind automated robotic recommendations and actions.
Core Methodology: Provides a comprehensive review of Deep Learning applications in Robot-Assisted Surgery: (1) Categorizes major image-guided surgical tasks including organ segmentation, surgical instrument detection, motion tracking, workflow recognition, and surgical skill evaluation; (2) Reviews state-of-the-art Deep Learning architectures including CNNs, RNNs, and GANs used for intraoperative guidance; (3) Examines real-time computer vision integration within robotic surgery platforms; and (4) Identifies technical, operational, and regulatory challenges associated with deploying AI-driven surgical assistance systems in clinical environments.

Critical Limitations: • Surgical data collection and annotation remain expensive, time-consuming, and limited due to privacy concerns and clinical constraints. • Lack of standardized validation protocols across different robotic surgery platforms restricts reproducibility and deployment scalability. • Black-box model behavior remains a major concern in safety-critical surgical environments where incorrect decisions may have catastrophic consequences.
Future Directions: • Develop lightweight, low-latency Deep Learning models suitable for real-time robotic deployment. • Advance Explainable AI techniques to improve transparency and surgeon trust in automated systems. • Promote multi-institutional data sharing initiatives to address dataset scarcity and improve model generalization. • Establish standardized benchmarking and validation frameworks across robotic surgery platforms.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly informs IoMT IDS research by highlighting one of the most safety-critical healthcare environments: Robot-Assisted Surgery. The study demonstrates that future IoMT intrusion detection systems must go beyond traditional network security and continuously verify the integrity of surgical video streams, robotic control commands, sensor feedback, and communication channels. An effective IDS must detect command injection, visual spoofing, sensor manipulation, and unauthorized robotic control attempts before they affect surgical operations, ensuring patient safety during real-time medical procedures.

Dataset: Systematic review of endoscopic image processing literature utilizing publicly available and clinical datasets including Kvasir-SEG, EndoVis, Cholec80, and other endoscopic imaging benchmarks used for lesion detection, surgical guidance, and image enhancement research.
Used Methods: Deep Learning (DL), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), U-Net, Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN), Image Segmentation, Image Classification, Image Enhancement, Multi-Task Learning, Unsupervised Learning, 3D Reconstruction.

Core Methodology: Provides a comprehensive review of Deep Learning applications in endoscopic imaging: (1) Examines image segmentation techniques for extracting polyps, lesions, and anatomical structures; (2) Reviews classification frameworks for gastrointestinal disease diagnosis including cancer and GERD detection; (3) Evaluates image enhancement methods such as denoising, super-resolution, and quality improvement; (4) Explores 3D reconstruction, object tracking, and real-time visual guidance for surgical procedures; and (5) Analyzes emerging trends including multi-task learning and unsupervised learning approaches for reducing annotation requirements.
Major Findings: • Deep Learning models significantly outperform traditional image-processing techniques in endoscopic lesion detection and classification tasks. • CNN-based architectures demonstrate superior feature extraction and pattern-recognition capabilities in complex clinical imaging environments. • Image enhancement techniques such as super-resolution and denoising substantially improve diagnostic quality in low-light and noisy endoscopic settings. • Multi-task and unsupervised learning approaches show strong potential for overcoming limitations associated with scarce annotated clinical data. • Advanced visual analytics contribute to improved surgical guidance and diagnostic accuracy.
Critical Limitations: • Deep Learning models remain highly dependent on large-scale annotated datasets that are difficult and expensive to obtain in healthcare environments. • Generalization across different endoscopic devices, imaging modalities, and clinical centers remains limited. • Black-box model behavior continues to restrict clinician trust and regulatory acceptance. • Performance may degrade when models are deployed outside their original training environments.
Future Directions: • Develop lightweight and interpretable Deep Learning architectures suitable for real-time clinical deployment. • Advance data-centric AI approaches including domain adaptation and unsupervised learning to reduce annotation requirements. • Improve cross-domain generalization across heterogeneous imaging platforms. • Strengthen Explainable AI techniques to increase clinician trust and regulatory acceptance.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly informs IoMT IDS research by highlighting the security challenges associated with high-resolution medical imaging pipelines. As AI-assisted endoscopic systems become increasingly integrated into connected healthcare infrastructures, IDS architectures must protect image acquisition, transmission, storage, and processing stages from adversarial manipulation. The study demonstrates the need for intrusion detection systems capable of identifying image-based adversarial attacks, data tampering, visual spoofing, and malicious perturbations that could deceive diagnostic AI models, ultimately safeguarding clinical decision-making and patient safety during diagnostic and surgical procedures.

Dataset: Simulated clinical sensor data including gas flow, oxygen concentration, airway pressure, patient vital signs, and anesthesia machine operational parameters used to validate an IoT-enabled anesthesia monitoring and management platform.
Used Methods: Internet of Things (IoT), Raspberry Pi Gateway, Cloud Computing, Remote Monitoring, HTTPS Communication, Mobile Healthcare Applications, Web-Based Control Systems, Medical Device Integration.
XAI: Does not explicitly implement Explainable AI techniques such as SHAP or LIME.
