Core Methodology: Proposes an IoT-based anesthesia management framework: (1) Utilizes Raspberry Pi as a central gateway to collect and aggregate data from anesthesia machine sensors; (2) Securely transmits physiological and operational data to cloud infrastructure using HTTPS communication protocols; (3) Provides web-based and mobile interfaces for remote monitoring and management by authorized medical staff; and (4) Supports centralized storage and retrieval of historical anesthesia records to improve clinical decision-making and operational efficiency.
Major Findings: • Enables real-time remote monitoring and control of anesthesia systems, improving clinical workflow efficiency and resource utilization. • Cloud-based infrastructure provides centralized access to historical patient and equipment records, facilitating evidence-based decision-making. • Secure communication protocols and access management mechanisms support regulatory compliance and patient data protection. • Remote accessibility improves operational flexibility, particularly in distributed healthcare environments. • Demonstrates the feasibility of integrating IoT technologies into critical care medical equipment management.
Critical Limitations: • Validation is based on simulated sensor data rather than live clinical deployment, limiting real-world generalizability. • Remote-control functionality introduces additional cybersecurity risks that could potentially affect patient safety if compromised. • The framework does not comprehensively evaluate resilience against sophisticated cyberattacks targeting medical device communication channels or control interfaces.
Future Directions: • Integrate machine learning and predictive analytics to support proactive anesthesia management and early risk detection. • Enable seamless interoperability with Electronic Health Record (EHR) systems to support comprehensive patient care. • Investigate advanced security architectures capable of protecting remote-control medical systems against emerging cyber threats. • Evaluate deployment under real-world clinical conditions involving live patient data and operational healthcare environments.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly informs IoMT IDS research by highlighting one of the most safety-critical attack surfaces in connected healthcare: remote control of medical devices. The study demonstrates that intrusion detection systems must continuously monitor command channels, authentication mechanisms, device-control interfaces, and cloud communication pathways to identify unauthorized access attempts, privilege escalation, command injection, or malicious parameter manipulation. Future IoMT IDS architectures must ensure that life-critical systems such as anesthesia machines remain both highly available and strongly protected against cyberattacks that could directly affect patient safety during medical procedures.

Dataset: 17,425 High-Frequency Ultrasound (HFUS) facial skin images obtained from 516 measurements across 44 patients, containing both informative and non-informative image frames for quality assessment and diagnostic evaluation.
Used Methods: Deep Learning (DL), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), VGG-16, Fuzzy Inference System (FIS), Image Quality Assessment (IQA), Grad-CAM, Medical Imaging Analytics, Automated Data Filtering.
XAI: Implements Explainable AI through Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), allowing clinicians to visualize the image regions influencing model decisions. The integration of Grad-CAM improves interpretability, transparency, and clinical trust by explaining why specific ultrasound frames are classified as informative or non-informative.
Core Methodology: Proposes an automated High-Frequency Ultrasound Image Quality Assessment framework: (1) Classifies ultrasound frames as informative or non-informative to remove noisy, corrupted, or diagnostically irrelevant images; (2) Utilizes a VGG-16 Convolutional Neural Network for binary and multi-class image quality classification; (3) Integrates a Fuzzy Inference System to refine classification confidence and generate quality scores; and (4) Uses Grad-CAM visualizations to provide explainable insights into the decision-making process.
Major Findings: • The proposed framework achieves up to 91.7% classification accuracy when identifying diagnostically useful HFUS images. • Automated image quality assessment significantly reduces manual frame selection workload and improves diagnostic reliability. • The integration of Fuzzy Inference Systems improves confidence estimation and classification robustness. • Grad-CAM explanations enhance clinician trust and transparency in automated image selection processes. • Performance remains stable across operators with varying levels of sonography expertise.
Critical Limitations: • Validation was limited primarily to facial skin ultrasound images, requiring broader evaluation across different anatomical regions and clinical scenarios. • Initial model development depends heavily on expert-labeled training datasets. • Generalization to other HFUS frequencies and pathological conditions remains insufficiently explored.
Future Directions: • Expand datasets to include additional body regions, disease conditions, and higher-frequency ultrasound imaging modalities. • Integrate FIS confidence measures directly into downstream segmentation, diagnostic, and decision-support systems. • Investigate more generalized and scalable image quality assessment frameworks for diverse clinical imaging environments. • Further enhance explainability mechanisms for clinical deployment.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly informs IoMT IDS research by introducing the concept of data-quality-aware security. The study demonstrates that not all incoming medical data should be automatically trusted, even when it originates from legitimate devices. Future IoMT intrusion detection systems should incorporate data quality validation mechanisms capable of identifying corrupted, noisy, manipulated, or low-information telemetry before it reaches downstream AI diagnostic models. This provides a valuable blueprint for detecting sensor malfunctions, transmission corruption, adversarial manipulation, or deliberate data poisoning attempts that may otherwise compromise clinical decision-making and patient safety.

Dataset: Systematic literature review of 63 peer-reviewed studies selected from SCOPUS, Web of Science, and PubMed databases, covering forensic science, artificial intelligence, digital forensics, biometrics, IoT, and emerging investigative technologies.
Used Methods: Systematic Literature Review (SLR), PRISMA Methodology, Quality Assessment, Cohen’s Kappa Analysis, Digital Forensics, Artificial Intelligence (AI), Big Data Analytics, Biometrics, Internet of Things (IoT), Extended Reality (XR).
XAI: Addresses explainability through human-centered forensic investigation rather than formal XAI frameworks. The study emphasizes that AI should function as a decision-support tool, while forensic experts retain responsibility for interpretation, validation, and evidential accountability. It highlights the importance of transparency, traceability, and legal defensibility when AI-generated conclusions are used in forensic contexts.
Core Methodology: Provides a comprehensive assessment of technological transformation in forensic science: (1) Categorizes emerging technologies into eleven domains including AI, Big Data, Biometrics, IoT, XR, and Digital Forensics; (2) Evaluates their impact across crime scene investigation, evidence collection, evidence preservation, laboratory analysis, and judicial processes; (3) Assesses operational, ethical, legal, and technical challenges associated with technology adoption; and (4) Examines how intelligent systems are reshaping forensic workflows and evidential management practices.
Major Findings: • Emerging technologies significantly improve the speed, accuracy, and scalability of forensic investigations. • AI and Big Data analytics enable efficient processing of massive evidence repositories that would be impractical for manual investigation. • IoT and wearable devices are becoming increasingly important sources of forensic evidence. • Advanced digitization technologies facilitate remote crime scene reconstruction, evidence preservation, and collaborative investigations. • The role of forensic professionals is evolving from manual evidence processing toward interpretation, validation, and expert decision-making.
Critical Limitations: • Legal and regulatory frameworks remain underdeveloped for many AI-driven forensic technologies, creating uncertainty regarding admissibility and evidential reliability. • High deployment costs and infrastructure requirements limit adoption across smaller forensic laboratories. • Significant training and expertise are required to effectively operate advanced forensic technologies. • Lack of standardization may create inconsistencies across jurisdictions and investigative organizations.
Future Directions: • Develop standardized legal, ethical, and operational frameworks for AI-assisted forensic investigations. • Expand Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR) training programs to improve forensic workforce capabilities. • Strengthen methodologies for preserving the authenticity, provenance, and integrity of IoT-generated evidence. • Improve interoperability and secure integration of wearable devices, IoT platforms, and forensic information systems.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly informs IoMT IDS research by emphasizing the growing forensic value of data generated by wearable devices, remote patient monitoring systems, and connected medical equipment. As healthcare IoMT ecosystems increasingly generate legally significant evidence, future IDS architectures must not only detect cyberattacks but also preserve data provenance, integrity, authenticity, and chain-of-custody. The study highlights the importance of developing forensic-ready IoMT security systems capable of identifying evidence tampering, unauthorized modifications, and integrity violations while maintaining legally defensible audit trails for clinical investigations and regulatory compliance.

Dataset: Utilizes large-scale healthcare datasets including MIMIC-III and other clinical vital-sign repositories containing elderly patient physiological records such as heart rate (HR), blood pressure (BP), and oxygen saturation (SpO2) measurements.
Used Methods: Deep Learning (DL), Time-Series Analysis, Anomaly Detection, Vital Sign Monitoring, Healthcare Analytics, Elderly Health Monitoring, Predictive Healthcare Intelligence.
XAI: Does not explicitly employ post-hoc explainability techniques such as SHAP or LIME. Instead, the study emphasizes clinically actionable anomaly detection by identifying abnormal physiological patterns that can support timely intervention by caregivers and healthcare professionals. The focus is on delivering reliable alerts rather than explaining individual model decisions.
Core Methodology: Proposes a Deep Learning-based abnormal vital-sign detection framework for elderly healthcare monitoring: (1) Collects and preprocesses continuous physiological measurements including heart rate, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation; (2) Utilizes deep neural network architectures to learn normal physiological behavior and identify deviations indicative of potential medical emergencies; (3) Performs real-time anomaly detection to support rapid clinical intervention; and (4) Validates effectiveness using large-scale healthcare datasets representative of elderly populations with diverse health conditions.
Major Findings: • Deep Learning-based anomaly detection demonstrates superior sensitivity compared with traditional threshold-based alert systems for identifying critical physiological abnormalities. • Real-time monitoring enables faster detection of potentially life-threatening conditions and supports timely medical intervention. • The framework maintains high detection performance across heterogeneous elderly patient populations with varying physiological characteristics. • Continuous monitoring improves the ability to identify subtle health deterioration patterns that may not be captured through periodic clinical assessments.
Critical Limitations: • Model performance depends heavily on continuous availability of high-quality physiological data streams. • Home-based monitoring environments may introduce missing values, sensor noise, communication failures, and incomplete data collection. • The framework focuses primarily on physiological anomalies and does not incorporate behavioral, contextual, or environmental information that may influence health outcomes. • Deep Learning models may introduce computational challenges for deployment on resource-constrained edge healthcare devices.
Future Directions: • Integrate behavioral monitoring, environmental sensing, and contextual health information to create more comprehensive elderly-care monitoring systems. • Develop lightweight Deep Learning architectures suitable for edge deployment on low-power IoMT devices. • Improve robustness against missing data, noisy sensor measurements, and communication disruptions common in home healthcare environments. • Investigate adaptive monitoring systems capable of personalizing anomaly thresholds based on individual patient characteristics.
Relevance to IoMT IDS Research: Directly informs IoMT IDS research by emphasizing the critical importance of availability and integrity within medical monitoring systems. In elderly healthcare environments, attacks such as data suppression, delay attacks, packet dropping, telemetry manipulation, or sensor spoofing could conceal life-threatening physiological events and prevent timely intervention. The study highlights that future IoMT IDS frameworks must prioritize protection of continuous vital-sign streams, ensuring that security mechanisms preserve the availability, timeliness, and integrity of life-critical healthcare telemetry while avoiding interference with emergency medical alerts.
